sentences.nl: Vertel wat Sem kan eten.
sentences.en: Tell what Sem can eat.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Vertel (Tell) wat (what) Sem (Sem) kan (can) eten (eat).  
• Natural English: Tell [me/us] what Sem can eat.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Imperative (Gebiedende wijs):** *Vertel* is the stem of *vertellen* (to tell). Placing it at the very beginning of the sentence without a subject creates a command or request.  
• **Subordinate Clause Word Order:** The word *wat* (what) introduces a dependent clause, which sends the verbs (*kan eten*) to the very end of the sentence.  
• **Modal Verbs in Subordinate Clauses:** In Dutch, you can place the modal verb before the infinitive (*kan eten*) or after it (*eten kan*) at the end of a subordinate clause. Put *kan* first is the most common in spoken Dutch.  
• **Extensions:**  
  – Vertel wat jij wilt doen. (Tell [me] what you want to do.)  
  – Ik weet wat hij moet kopen. (I know what he has to buy.)  
  – Vraag wat zij mag drinken. (Ask what she is allowed to drink.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Laat zien wat Anna kan maken. (Show what Anna can make.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• *Sem* is a very popular, modern Dutch first name (most commonly for boys, derived from Samuel). Additionally, using the direct imperative (*Vertel...*) is normal in Dutch and is not considered rude among friends, family, or colleagues, unlike in English where it often requires softening ("Could you tell me...").

vertel.form_note: imperative (command form) of 'vertellen', same as the ik-form in the present tense; frequently used in A2 speaking exams to introduce an indirect question
vertel.fast_speech: initial /v/ is often pronounced voiceless like /f/: /fərˈtɛl/

wat.form_note: interrogative pronoun introducing an indirect question (subordinate clause) after 'Vertel'; sends all verbs ('kan eten') to the end of the sentence, though in your exam answer you must switch back to verb-second word order (e.g. 'Sem kan...')

sem.form_note: subject of the subordinate clause; in your exam answer, start with 'Sem' or 'Hij' followed immediately by the conjugated verb 'kan'

kan.form_note: 3rd person singular (hij/Sem) present tense of the irregular modal verb 'kunnen'; placed near the end because of the indirect question 'wat', and reusable in your answer in the second position ('Sem kan...')

eten.form_note: infinitive of 'eten', paired with the modal verb 'kan' at the end of the clause; when answering with 'kan', keep 'eten' at the very end of your main clause (e.g. 'Sem kan een appel eten')

grammarHits.explanation: Both verbs go to the end: kan eten.

sentences.nl: Vertel ook wat u van dit eten vindt.
sentences.en: Also tell what you think of this food.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Vertel (Tell) / ook (also) / wat (what) / u (you - formal) / van (of) / dit (this) / eten (food) / vindt (find/think).  
• Natural translation: Also tell [us/me] what you think of this food.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Imperative Mood:** *Vertel* is the command form of the verb *vertellen* (to tell). It is formed by using the verb stem, placed at the very beginning of the sentence.  
• **Idiom (*vinden van*):** In Dutch, to ask or state an opinion ("to think of"), you use the verb *vinden* (literally "to find") combined with the preposition *van* (of/from).  
• **Subordinate Clause Word Order:** The word *wat* introduces an indirect question (a subordinate clause), which forces the conjugated verb (*vindt*) all the way to the end of the sentence.  
• **Demonstrative Pronoun (*dit*):** *Eten* (food) is a *het*-word (neuter), so "this" translates to *dit* (rather than *deze*, which is used for *de*-words).  

• **Extensions:**  
– Vertel me wat je van deze film vindt. (Tell me what you think of this movie.)  
– Ik weet niet wat zij van het nieuwe plan vindt. (I don't know what she thinks of the new plan.)  
– Laat ook weten wat u van onze service vindt. (Also let [us] know what you think of our service.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Vertel ons ook wat u van de nieuwe auto vindt. (Also tell us what you think of the new car.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• **Dutch Directness & Hospitality:** Using the formal *u* combined with asking about the food is very common in restaurants, surveys, or when hosting guests you don't know intimately. Because Dutch culture values directness and honesty, if someone asks what you *vindt van* the food, they generally appreciate a genuine answer rather than overly effusive, polite praise—though it is still polite to be constructive!

vertel.form_note: imperative (command form) of 'vertellen' (uses the verb stem). On the A2 speaking exam, prompts starting with 'Vertel...' introduce an indirect question.
vertel.fast_speech: The prefix 'ver-' is unstressed and reduced to /vər/ or /və/.

ook.form_note: connective adverb; signals that this is the second part of the exam prompt that you must answer.

wat.form_note: interrogative pronoun introducing an indirect question (subordinate clause) after 'Vertel'. Because it starts a subordinate clause, the conjugated verb ('vindt') is pushed to the very end of the sentence.

u.form_note: 2nd person singular/plural formal subject pronoun. When you answer the question, change 'u' to 'ik' (e.g., 'Ik vind...').

van.form_note: fixed preposition used with the verb 'vinden' ('iets vinden van' = to have an opinion about something). Reuse both 'vinden' and 'van' in your answer.
van.fast_speech: Often pronounced with a voiceless /f/ at the start: /fɑn/.

dit.form_note: singular proximate demonstrative used before 'het'-words (neuter nouns) like 'het eten'.

eten.form_note: singular uncountable neuter noun ('het eten'), derived from the verb infinitive 'eten' (to eat); has no plural form.

vindt.form_note: 2nd person singular formal ('u') present tense of 'vinden': stem 'vind' + '-t'. Placed at the end of the sentence because it is in an indirect question after 'wat'. In your exam answer, reuse this verb in the 2nd position with 'ik': 'Ik vind dit eten lekker, want...'.
vindt.fast_speech: The '-dt' ending is pronounced as a single /t/ sound, identical to 'ik vind' (/vɪnt/).

sentences.nl: Gebruik het plaatje.
sentences.en: Use the picture.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Gebruik = Use  
• het = the  
• plaatje = picture / image  
• Natural translation: Use the picture.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Imperative (Gebiedende wijs):** *Gebruik* is the imperative (command) form of the verb *gebruiken* (to use). In Dutch, commands are formed simply by using the verb stem (the *ik*-form) at the very beginning of the sentence, with no subject pronoun.  
• **Diminutive and Article:** *Plaatje* is the diminutive form of *de plaat* (plate/panel/print), created by adding the suffix *-je*. In Dutch, *all* diminutive singular nouns become neuter and take the article *het*, regardless of the base word's original gender. While it literally means "little plate," *het plaatje* is the standard everyday word for a small picture, illustration, or image.  
• **Extensions:**  
– Gebruik een pen. (Use a pen.)  
– Bekijk het plaatje. (Look at the picture.)  
– Gebruik het woordenboek niet. (Do not use the dictionary.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Gebruik de tekst om de vragen te beantwoorden. (Use the text to answer the questions.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• *Plaatje* is also used in a very common Dutch idiom: *Het totale plaatje* or *het hele plaatje* ("the whole picture"), used when talking about considering all aspects of a situation (e.g., job benefits, a house). Furthermore, calling someone or something *een plaatje* ("a picture") is a common way to say they look gorgeous or picture-perfect!

sentences.nl: Verschillende soorten groenten.
sentences.en: Different kinds of vegetables.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Verschillende = Different / various  
• soorten = types / kinds  
• groenten = vegetables  
• (Full meaning: "Different kinds of vegetables.")

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **No "van" needed:** In English, we say "kinds *of* vegetables," using a preposition. In Dutch, when expressing a type, sort, or measure of something, you simply place the nouns right next to each other without *van* (of).  
• **Adjective Ending (-e):** The adjective *verschillend* (different) gets an **-e** at the end (*verschillende*) because it modifies a plural noun (*soorten*).  
• **Plural Forms:** Both *soort* (soorten) and *groente* (groenten) are in their plural forms here. Note that *groente* is often used in the singular as a collective noun (e.g., *veel groente* = lots of vegetables), but when talking about different *types*, the plural *groenten* is preferred.  
• **Extensions:**  
– *Drie soorten kaas.* (Three kinds of cheese.)  
– *Verschillende maten schoenen.* (Different sizes of shoes.)  
– *Alle soorten muziek.* (All kinds of music.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Deze winkel verkoopt veel verschillende soorten fruit en groenten. (This shop sells many different kinds of fruit and vegetables.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch supermarkets, it is extremely common to find *voorgesneden groenten* (pre-cut vegetables) mixed into bags for specific dishes, such as *soepgroenten* (soup vegetables), *roerbakgroenten* (stir-fry vegetables), or *macaronigroenten* (vegetables for pasta). This reflects the practical, time-saving approach the Dutch often take toward weekday cooking.

verschillende.form_note: inflected adjective with -e ending because it modifies the plural noun 'soorten'

soorten.form_note: plural of soort: add -en. In Dutch, no preposition like 'van' (of) is needed between 'soorten' and the noun that follows

groenten.form_note: plural of groente: ends in -e, so add -n (groentes is also a valid plural). Note: this whole phrase is a short fragment without a verb; on the A2 speaking exam it is better to make a full sentence by reusing the question's verb, e.g., 'Ik eet verschillende soorten groenten.'

sentences.nl: De groenten zien er goed uit.
sentences.en: The vegetables look good.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• De (The) groenten (vegetables) zien (see) er (there) goed (good) uit (out).  
• Natural meaning: "The vegetables look good."

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Er ... uitzien (To look/appear):** This is a separable verb (*uitzien*) always combined with the word *er*. In a main clause, the verb stem (*zien* for plural) goes to the second position, and the prefix (*uit*) goes to the very end of the sentence. The adjective describing the appearance goes right before *uit*.  
• **Er + Adjective:** Notice that *er* is separated from *uit* here. If there is no extra information or just a short adjective, they can sometimes be written together (*eruit*), like in a question, but with an adjective like *goed*, they split: *er [adjective] uit*.  
• **Plural Noun:** *Groente* (vegetable) takes an *-n* to become plural (*groenten*), which requires the plural verb form *zien*.  

• **Extensions:**  
– Je ziet er moe uit. (You look tired.)  
– Het weer ziet er slecht uit vandaag. (The weather looks bad today.)  
– Hoe ziet jouw nieuwe auto eruit? (What does your new car look like?)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Dat verse brood ziet er heerlijk uit. (That fresh bread looks delicious.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch supermarkets, it is very common to find *voorgesneden groenten* (pre-cut and washed vegetables) in bags. Dutch food culture values convenience and efficiency for weekday meals, so checking if the bagged vegetables "zien er goed uit" (look fresh) is a daily habit for many shoppers.

sentences.nl: Sem kan sla, tomaatjes, paprika en komkommer eten.
sentences.en: Sem can eat lettuce, little tomatoes, bell pepper, and cucumber.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **Sem** – Sem  
• **kan** – can  
• **sla,** – lettuce,  
• **tomaatjes,** – little tomatoes (cherry tomatoes),  
• **paprika** – bell pepper  
• **en** – and  
• **komkommer** – cucumber  
• **eten.** – to eat.  
*(Natural translation: Sem can eat lettuce, cherry tomatoes, bell pepper, and cucumber.)*

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Modal Verbs and the "Verb Bracket":** *Kan* comes from the modal verb *kunnen* (can / to be able to). In a Dutch main clause, the conjugated modal verb goes in the second position (right after the subject), and the main action verb (*eten*) is pushed to the very end of the sentence in its infinitive form. Everything else goes in the middle.  
• **Diminutives:** *Tomaatjes* is the plural diminutive of *tomaat* (tomato). Adding *-je(s)* makes something small. In the context of food, *tomaatjes* specifically refers to cherry or grape tomatoes.  
• **Collective Singulars:** Notice that *sla*, *paprika*, and *komkommer* are in the singular form. In Dutch, when listing vegetables as general food types or ingredients, it is very common to use the singular form rather than the plural.  

**Extensions:**  
• Ik kan vandaag verse groenten kopen. (I can buy fresh vegetables today.)  
• Zij kan heel goed koken. (She can cook very well.)  
• Wij eten vanavond sla met komkommer en tomaatjes. (We are eating lettuce with cucumber and cherry tomatoes tonight.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Mila kan een salade met paprika en komkommer maken. (Mila can make a salad with bell pepper and cucumber.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• **False Friend Alert:** In Dutch, *paprika* always means sweet bell pepper (red, yellow, green, or orange), never the spicy chili pepper (which is a *Spaanse peper* or *chilipeper*). However, the Dutch are famously obsessed with *paprikachips*—potato chips flavored with sweet bell pepper seasoning, which is the most popular chip flavor in the country!  
• **Snackgroenten:** Raw vegetables like *tomaatjes*, *komkommer*, and *paprika* are known as *snackgroenten* (snack vegetables). It is standard practice at Dutch primary schools for children to bring a small container of these to eat during their 10:00 AM break (*het tienuurtje*).

sla.form_note: singular uncountable de-noun, first item in the direct object list

paprika.form_note: singular de-noun, used here as an uncountable food item in the direct object list

en.form_note: coordinating conjunction connecting the last two nouns in the list
en.fast_speech: often reduced to /ən/ or /n/

eten.form_note: infinitive of the strong verb 'eten', placed at the very end of the sentence because it is paired with the modal verb 'kan'

sentences.nl: Het is gezond, maar ik mis de rijst.
sentences.en: It is healthy, but I miss the rice.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Het (It) is (is) gezond (healthy), maar (but) ik (I) mis (miss) de (the) rijst (rice).  
• Natural translation: It is healthy, but I miss the rice.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Coordinating Conjunction ("maar"):** *Maar* (but) is a coordinating conjunction. Unlike subordinating conjunctions (like *omdat* or *dat*), *maar* does not change the word order of the following clause. The second part simply follows the normal Subject + Verb + Object structure (*ik mis de rijst*).  
• **Predicate Adjective:** Because *gezond* (healthy) comes after the linking verb *is* and doesn't sit directly in front of a noun, it stays in its base form and does not take an *-e* ending.  
• **Definite Article:** *Rijst* is a *de*-word (common gender). In Dutch, when referring to a specific component of a meal that you usually expect to be there, using the definite article (*de*) is very natural.

**Extensions:**  
• Het is lekker, maar ik mis het zout. (It is tasty, but I miss the salt.)  
• De soep is warm, maar ik mis het brood. (The soup is warm, but I miss the bread.)  
• Het is goedkoop, maar ik mis de kwaliteit. (It is cheap, but I miss the quality.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Deze salade is erg vers, maar ik mis de kaas. (This salad is very fresh, but I miss the cheese.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• While traditional Dutch dinners revolve around the *AVG'tje* (Aardappelen, Vlees, Groente – potatoes, meat, vegetables), rice has been a massive staple in the Netherlands for generations due to its colonial history with Indonesia and Suriname. Dish styles like *nasi goreng* or a *rijsttafel* (rice table) are deeply embedded in Dutch food culture. However, with modern health trends like low-carb diets (*koolhydraatarm eten*) replacing rice with cauliflower rice or extra vegetables, this exact sentence is something you might frequently hear at a modern Dutch dinner table!

sentences.nl: Ik zie een saladebar.
sentences.en: I see a salad bar.
sentences.note: Meester's reference answer, built from the topic bank.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **Ik** – I  
• **zie** – see  
• **een** – a  
• **saladebar.** – salad bar.  

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Word Order (SVO):** This sentence follows the standard Subject-Verb-Object structure used in simple Dutch main clauses.  
• **Verb Conjugation:** *Zie* is the first-person singular (ik) present tense of the irregular verb *zien* (to see).  
• **Compound Noun:** *Saladebar* is a compound word combining *salade* (salad) and *bar* (bar). In Dutch, compound nouns are written together as one word. It is a *de*-word (*de saladebar*), though the indefinite article *een* (a/an) is used for both *de* and *het* words.  
• **Extensions:**  
  – *Ik zie een leuk restaurant.* (I see a nice restaurant.)  
  – *Zie jij de saladebar?* (Do you see the salad bar?)  
  – *Wij zien een grote supermarkt.* (We see a big supermarket.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• *Ik zoek een goede saladebar in het centrum.* (I am looking for a good salad bar in the city center.)  

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Large Dutch supermarkets (especially *Albert Heijn To Go* at train stations or larger *Jumbo* stores) frequently feature self-service salad bars where commuters and students assemble fresh lunches on the go.

sentences.en: Sem can eat lettuce, little tomatoes, bell pepper, and cucumber.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Sem = Sem  
• kan = can  
• sla = lettuce  
• tomaatjes = little tomatoes  
• paprika = bell pepper  
• en = and  
• komkommer = cucumber  
• eten = eat  

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Modal Verb Sentence Bracket:** When using a modal verb like *kunnen* (can/to be able to), the conjugated modal verb (*kan*) goes in the second position, and the main verb in its infinitive form (*eten*) is pushed to the very end of the sentence. Everything else goes in the middle.  
• **Diminutives (*Verkleinwoorden*):** *Tomaatjes* is the plural diminutive of *tomaat* (tomato + *-je* + *-s*). In Dutch, this is the standard way to refer to cherry tomatoes or snack tomatoes.  
• **False Friend Alert:** *Paprika* in Dutch means "bell pepper" (sweet pepper), not the spice paprika (which is called *paprikapoeder*).  

**Extensions:**  
• Ik kan vandaag vers fruit en groenten kopen. (I can buy fresh fruit and vegetables today.)  
• Kun jij de komkommer en de tomaatjes snijden? (Can you cut the cucumber and the little tomatoes?)  
• Wij kunnen vanavond een lekkere salade maken. (We can make a tasty salad tonight.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Mijn dochter kan appel, banaan en druifjes eten. (My daughter can eat apple, banana, and little grapes.)  

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• **Snackgroenten (Snack Vegetables):** Raw vegetables like *tomaatjes*, *komkommer*, and *paprika* are staples in Dutch school lunchboxes (alongside a *boterham* or sandwich) and are also commonly served as healthy afternoon snacks for children (*tussendoortjes*) or on party tables to balance out heavier fried snacks.  
• **No Oxford Comma:** In Dutch, you generally do not put a comma before the word *en* (and) at the end of a list.

sentences.nl: Ik vind het lekker, want het is gezond.
sentences.en: I think it is tasty, because it is healthy.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Ik = I  
• vind = find  
• het = it  
• lekker, = tasty,  
• want = because / for  
• het = it  
• is = is  
• gezond. = healthy.  

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Ik vind het + [adjective]:** The verb *vinden* (to find) is commonly used in Dutch to express an opinion ("I think it is...").  
• **Word order with *want*:** *Want* (because) is a coordinating conjunction. Unlike *omdat* (which sends the verb to the end of the clause), *want* keeps the standard main clause word order: Subject (*het*) + Verb (*is*) + Adjective (*gezond*).  
• **Extensions:**  
– Ik vind het duur, want ik heb geen geld. (I think it is expensive, because I have no money.)  
– Zij vindt de soep lekker. (She thinks the soup is tasty / She likes the soup.)  
– Wij eten veel fruit, want dat is gezond. (We eat a lot of fruit, because that is healthy.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Ik drink graag groene thee, want het is heel gezond. (I like drinking green tea, because it is very healthy.)  

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• The word **lekker** is one of the most versatile and frequently used words in the Netherlands. While it translates to "tasty" for food, the Dutch use it for almost anything that feels good or pleasant, such as *lekker slapen* (sleeping well), *lekker weer* (nice weather), or *lekker makkelijk* (nice and easy).

sentences.nl: Kijk naar het plaatje.
sentences.en: Look at the picture.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Kijk = Look  
• naar = at / towards  
• het = the (neuter)  
• plaatje = little picture / image  

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Imperative Mood:** *Kijk* is the command form (imperative) of the verb *kijken* (to look). In Dutch, the imperative for a singular or general audience is simply the verb stem (infinitive minus *-en*) placed at the very beginning of the sentence.  
• **Fixed Preposition:** Just as English uses "look *at*", Dutch uses the fixed combination *kijken naar*.  
• **Diminutive Noun:** *Plaatje* is the diminutive form of *de plaat* (plate/print/record). Adding the suffix *-je* makes a noun smaller or more specific, and grammatically changes all nouns to neuter gender, which is why it uses the article *het*.  

• Kijk naar de camera. (Look at the camera.)  
• Luister naar het liedje. (Listen to the song.)  
• Kijk eens naar dit plaatje. (Just take a look at this picture.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Kijk naar het bord voor het juiste antwoord. (Look at the board for the correct answer.)  

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• While *plaatje* literally means "little picture" and is standard in textbooks or classrooms, it is also used idiomatically in everyday Dutch. Saying *"Het is een plaatje!"* (It's a little picture!) means something or someone is "picture-perfect" or stunningly beautiful, often used to compliment a bride, a well-dressed child, or a nicely renovated room.

sentences.nl: Jafar komt te laat op zijn werk.
sentences.en: Jafar arrives late at his work.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Jafar (Jafar) / komt (comes / arrives) / te laat (too late) / op (on / at) / zijn (his) / werk (work).  
• Natural translation: Jafar arrives late at work.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Te laat komen:** In English, you simply say "to be late" or "to arrive late," while Dutch requires the adverb *te* (too) to express lateness (*te laat*). Using *komen* (to come) rather than *zijn* (to be) emphasizes the action of arriving.  
• **Preposition *op*:** In Dutch, the preposition *op* (literally "on") is commonly used to mean "at" for institutions, events, or public spaces like work (*op het werk*), school (*op school*), or a party (*op een feestje*).  
• **Extensions:**  
  – Ik ben te laat voor de vergadering. (I am late for the meeting.)  
  – Zij is al op haar werk. (She is already at work.)  
  – De trein komt vijf minuten te laat. (The train arrives five minutes late.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Door de file komt Eva vandaag te laat op school. (Because of the traffic jam, Eva is arriving late at school today.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Punctuality (*stiptheid*) is very important in Dutch culture, both professionally and socially. Being on time (*op tijd*) often means arriving five to ten minutes early. If you know you are going to be *te laat*—even by just five minutes—it is standard etiquette to immediately message or call to let the other person know.

sentences.nl: Waarom komt hij te laat?
sentences.en: Why does he arrive late?
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **Waarom** (Why) **komt** (comes) **hij** (he) **te** (too) **laat?** (late?)  
• Natural translation: Why is he late?

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Verb Choice (Komen vs. Zijn):** Where English uses "to be late," Dutch often uses the verb *komen* (to come) combined with *te laat* (too late) when referring to arriving somewhere after the scheduled time.  
• **Word Order (Inversion):** In a question starting with a question word (*waarom*), the verb (*komt*) must come immediately second, followed by the subject (*hij*).  
• **Te laat:** Literally "too late," this is the standard Dutch way to simply say "late."  
• **Extensions:**  
  – Waarom ga je zo vroeg? (Why are you leaving/going so early?)  
  – Hij komt altijd op tijd. (He is always on time / He always arrives on time.)  
  – Sorry dat ik te laat kom. (Sorry that I am [arriving] late.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Waarom komt de trein vandaag zo laat? (Why is the train so late today?)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• **Punctuality:** The Dutch value punctuality highly. Being even 5 to 10 minutes *te laat* for a meeting, appointment, or social gathering without calling ahead is generally considered rude. Conversely, arriving *op tijd* (on time) is the expected norm.

waarom.form_note: interrogative adverb asking for a reason; at the A2 exam, you almost always answer a 'waarom' question using the conjunction 'omdat' (verb goes to the end) or 'want' (normal verb-second main clause: 'Hij komt te laat, want...')

komt.form_note: 3rd person singular (hij) present tense of the irregular verb 'komen' (stem 'kom' + -t). Placed before the subject 'hij' because of question inversion; when answering, reuse this verb in second position: 'Hij komt te laat, want...'

hij.form_note: 3rd person singular masculine subject pronoun; placed after the verb 'komt' in questions, but moves to first position in your answer ('Hij komt...')
hij.fast_speech: after a verb ending in -t, unstressed 'hij' often becomes '-ie' in spoken Dutch: 'Waarom komt-ie te laat?' /ˈkɔmti/

te.form_note: adverb of degree modifying 'laat'; in Dutch, arriving late for an appointment is always expressed as 'te laat komen' (literally: to come too late)

laat.form_note: base form of the adjective/adverb 'laat', used adverbially here with 'te' in the fixed expression 'te laat komen' (to arrive late)

sentences.nl: Vertel ook wat hij nu moet doen.
sentences.en: Also tell what he has to do now.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Vertel (Tell) | ook (also) | wat (what) | hij (he) | nu (now) | moet (must) | doen (do).

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Imperative (Command):** *Vertel* is the stem of the verb *vertellen* (to tell). Starting a sentence with the verb stem creates a direct command.  
• **Indirect Question (Subordinate Clause):** The word *wat* (what) introduces a subordinate clause. In Dutch, this pushes all the verbs in that clause to the very end: *...wat hij nu **moet doen**.*  
• **End-cluster Verb Order:** When a modal verb (*moet*) and an infinitive (*doen*) are pushed to the end of a clause, standard Dutch normally puts theconjugated modal verb first (*moet doen*), though the reverse (*doen moet*) is also grammatically acceptable.

**Extensions:**  
• *Laat me weten wat ik morgen moet meenemen.* (Let me know what I must bring tomorrow.)  
• *Vraag ook waar zij precies woont.* (Also ask where she lives exactly.)  
• *Ik weet niet wat we nu moeten zeggen.* (I don't know what we must say now.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Leg ook uit waarom we vandaag moeten wachten. (Also explain why we have to wait today.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Dutch communication is famously direct. Using an unsoftened imperative like *Vertel...* (Tell...) is completely normal and polite enough in everyday contexts or work emails in the Netherlands, whereas English speakers might feel the need to soften it with "Could you also tell..." or "Please tell...".

vertel.form_note: Singular imperative (command form) of the inseparable verb 'vertellen' (uses the verb stem, which is the same as the 1st person singular present). In the A2 speaking exam, prompts often start with 'Vertel...' followed by an indirect question; to answer, you turn the indirect clause back into a normal main clause.
vertel.fast_speech: The prefix 'ver-' is unstressed and reduced: /vərˈtɛl/ or /fərˈtɛl/.

ook.form_note: Adverb modifying the command 'vertel', instructing you to add a second piece of information in your exam answer.

wat.form_note: Introduces the indirect question after 'Vertel'. Because 'wat' makes this a subordinate clause, all verbs ('moet doen') are pushed to the very end of the sentence.

hij.form_note: 3rd person singular masculine subject pronoun. In your exam answer, start your sentence with 'Hij' and put the conjugated verb immediately second: 'Hij moet...'
hij.fast_speech: When unstressed in the middle of a sentence, often pronounced /i/ (so 'wat hij' sounds like /ˈʋɑti/).

nu.form_note: Time adverb placed in the middle field before the final verb cluster.

moet.form_note: 3rd person singular ('hij') present tense of the modal verb 'moeten'. Note that modal verbs do not add an extra -t in the 'hij' form when the stem already ends in -t. Placed near the end because of the indirect question after 'Vertel... wat'; when you answer in a main clause, reuse 'moet' in the second position ('Hij moet nu...').
moet.fast_speech: Before 'doen', the /t/ assimilates to /d/ and merges: 'moet doen' sounds like /muˈdun/.

doen.form_note: Infinitive of 'doen', paired with the modal verb 'moet' at the end of the clause. When answering this exam question, you replace 'doen' with a specific action infinitive at the very end of your sentence (e.g., 'Hij moet nu werken').

grammarHits.highlight: Vertel ook wat hij nu moet doen
grammarHits.explanation: moet doen at the end: what he has to do now.

sentences.nl: Ik zie veel auto's op de weg.
sentences.en: I see many cars on the road.
sentences.note: Meester's reference answer, built from the topic bank.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **Ik** (I) **zie** (see) **veel** (many) **auto's** (cars) **op** (on) **de** (the) **weg** (road).

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Verb Conjugation:** *Zie* is the first-person singular (ik) form of the irregular verb *zien* (to see).  
• **Plural with Apostrophe:** *Auto's* uses an apostrophe + *s* to form the plural. In Dutch, nouns ending in a single long vowel (like -a, -i, -o, -u, -y) take *'s* so the vowel sound remains long. Without the apostrophe (*autos*), the 'o' would be pronounced short.  
• **Preposition:** In Dutch, traffic is **op** (on) the road (*op de weg*) or **op** the street (*op straat*), rather than "in" the street.  

• **Extensions:**  
  – Ik zie veel fietsen op straat. (I see many bicycles on the street.)  
  – Wij zien twee foto's op de tafel. (We see two photos on the table.)  
  – Zie jij veel mensen in het park? (Do you see many people in the park?)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Zij ziet veel paraplu's op het plein. (She sees many umbrellas on the square.)  

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• The Netherlands is one of the most densely populated countries in the world, so seeing "many cars on the road" is a daily reality. The Dutch have a specific word for a traffic jam, **de file**, and discussing *files* during the morning commute is a national pastime right alongside talking about the weather.

ik.form_note: 1st person singular subject pronoun; starts the main clause in position 1
ik.fast_speech: unstressed often reduced to /ək/

zie.form_note: 1st person singular present tense of 'zien'; sits in position 2 (verb-second rule) and reuses the exam question's verb ('Wat zie je op het plaatje?')

veel.form_note: uninflected quantifier before the plural noun 'auto's'

auto's.form_note: plural of auto: add 's with an apostrophe to keep the long -o sound; functions as the direct object

op.form_note: preposition of place introducing the location 'op de weg'
op.fast_speech: before 'de', the /p/ is often unreleased or voiced to /b/: /ɔb də/

de.form_note: definite article for singular common-gender nouns (de-words) like 'weg'

weg.form_note: singular noun; object of the preposition 'op' (note: the vowel lengthens in the plural 'wegen')

sentences.nl: Jafar staat in de file.
sentences.en: Jafar is stuck in a traffic jam.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Jafar = Jafar  
• staat = stands (is standing)  
• in = in  
• de = the  
• file = traffic jam  
• *Natural translation: Jafar is stuck in a traffic jam.*

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Posture Verbs:** Dutch strongly prefers using specific posture verbs (*staan* - to stand, *liggen* - to lie, *zitten* - to sit) where English simply uses "to be" or "to be stuck." Even though Jafar is physically sitting in his car, the cars as a collective are "standing" still on the road, so the fixed idiom is *in de file staan*.  
• **Preposition:** The correct preposition here is *in*, just like in English ("in a traffic jam").  
• **Extensions:**  
  – Ik sta in de rij. (I am standing in line / queuing.)  
  – Er staat een lange file op de A2. (There is a long traffic jam on the A2 highway.)  
  – Hoe lang sta je al in de file? (How long have you been stuck in traffic?)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Sorry dat ik te laat ben, maar ik stond een uur in de file. (Sorry that I am late, but I was stuck in a traffic jam for an hour.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• The Netherlands is very densely populated, making *de file* a daily reality and a favorite topic of small talk (right after the weather). Excusing yourself for being late because you *stond in de file* is widely accepted, and Dutch radio stations broadcast *filemeldingen* (traffic jam reports) every half hour during rush hour (*de spits*).

jafar.form_note: subject of the sentence, placed in first position

staat.meaning: stands / is stuck (in the expression 'in de file staan')
staat.form_note: 3rd person singular present tense of 'staan'; placed in second position (verb-second word order)

in.form_note: fixed preposition used in the expression 'in de file staan' (to be stuck in a traffic jam)

de.form_note: common-gender singular definite article going with the de-word 'file'

file.form_note: singular common-gender noun (de-word); French loanword, so the final -e is pronounced as a schwa

sentences.nl: Hij moet zijn baas bellen.
sentences.en: He has to call his boss.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Hij (He) + moet (must) + zijn (his) + baas (boss) + bellen (to call).

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Modal Verbs & Word Order:** *Moet* is the singular form of *moeten* (must/have to). In a Dutch main clause, the conjugated modal verb sits in the second position, and the main action verb (*bellen*) is pushed to the very end of the sentence in its infinitive form.  
• **Direct Object vs. Preposition:** Unlike English where you sometimes say "call *to* someone," *bellen* takes a direct object here (*zijn baas*), just like "to call someone." (Note: *bellen met* is also used to mean "talking on the phone with").  
• **Extensions:**  
– Ik moet mijn moeder bellen. (I have to call my mother.)  
– Zij moet vandaag werken. (She has to work today.)  
– Wij moeten de dokter bellen. (We must call the doctor.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Jij moet morgen je nieuwe collega bellen. (You have to call your new colleague tomorrow.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Dutch workplace culture is famous for its flat hierarchies. Even though the word *baas* (boss) is used casually, managers are treated as equals rather than superiors. Calling your boss in the Netherlands is typically an informal affair where you use their first name and the informal "you" (*je/jij*).

hij.form_note: 3rd person singular masculine subject pronoun; starts the sentence in position 1
hij.fast_speech: when unstressed (usually after a verb), often pronounced /i/ (spelled 'ie')

moet.form_note: 3rd person singular present tense of the modal verb 'moeten'; sits in position 2 (verb-second rule) and sends the main verb 'bellen' to the end of the sentence

zijn.form_note: 3rd person singular masculine possessive pronoun modifying 'baas'
zijn.fast_speech: almost always reduced to /zə(n)/ (often written z'n) in natural speech

baas.form_note: singular common-gender (de) noun, acting as the direct object of 'bellen'
word_forms: plural: bazen (s becomes z, long vowel written with one 'a' in open syllable, add -en)

bellen.form_note: infinitive of 'bellen'; placed at the very end of the sentence because of the modal verb 'moet' in position 2

grammarHits.explanation: moet is second; bellen goes to the end.

sentences.nl: Kijk naar het plaatje.
sentences.en: Look at the picture.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Kijk = Look  
• naar = at / towards  
• het = the  
• plaatje = (little) picture / image  
• Natural meaning: "Look at the picture."

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Imperative Mood (Command):** *Kijk* is the stem of the verb *kijken* (to look). In Dutch, you form a basic command by putting the verb stem at the very beginning of the sentence without a subject pronoun.  
• **Fixed Preposition:** Just as English uses "look *at*," Dutch pairs the verb *kijken* with the preposition *naar* (*kijken naar* = to look at / to watch).  
• **Diminutive & Gender:** *Plaatje* is the diminutive form of *de plaat* (plate/print/record). Because it has the diminutive suffix *-je*, its article automatically changes to *het*. In everyday Dutch, *plaatje* is the standard word for an illustration or small picture.  

• **Extensions:**  
– Kijk naar de televisie. (Look at / Watch the television.)  
– Luister naar het verhaal. (Listen to the story.)  
– Wij kijken naar de mooie plaatjes in het boek. (We are looking at the pretty pictures in the book.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Kijk naar die grappige hond op straat! (Look at that funny dog on the street!)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• *Plaatje* is also used idiomatically in Dutch. If something looks picture-perfect (like a person dressed up nicely, a well-decorated room, or a cute baby), Dutch people will often say: *"Het is een plaatje!"* ("It's a picture!" / "It's gorgeous!"). You will also see this exact sentence (*Kijk naar het plaatje*) constantly in Dutch language textbooks and civic integration exams (*inburgeringsexamen*).

kijk.form_note: imperative singular of kijken (formed with the verb stem); commands start with the verb in first position

naar.form_note: fixed preposition used with kijken: kijken naar = to look at
naar.fast_speech: often reduced to /nər/ in unstressed position

het.form_note: definite article for singular neuter (het-words); all diminutive nouns ending in -je take het
het.fast_speech: almost always pronounced /ət/ in natural speech

plaatje.form_note: singular diminutive of de plaat (plate/record/large print): add -je; makes the noun a het-word

sentences.nl: Wat doet de vrouw?
sentences.en: What is the woman doing?
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Wat = What  
• doet = does / is doing  
• de = the  
• vrouw = woman  
• Natural translation: What is the woman doing? (or: What does the woman do?)

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Question Word Order (Inversion):** In Dutch, when a question starts with a question word like *wat* (what), the verb comes immediately second, followed by the subject (*de vrouw*).  
• **Present Tense:** Dutch uses the simple present tense (*doet*, from the infinitive *doen*) to express both the English continuous present ("is doing") and simple present ("does").  
• **Gender/Article:** *Vrouw* is a common-gender noun, so it takes the definite article *de* (the).  

**Extensions:**  
• Wat doet de man? (What is the man doing?)  
• Wat ziet de vrouw? (What does the woman see?)  
• Waar woont de vrouw? (Where does the woman live?)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Wat leest de vrouw in het park? (What is the woman reading in the park?)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Asking someone "Wat doe je?" (or about someone else, "Wat doet de vrouw?") is the standard way in the Netherlands to ask what someone does for a living, just like "What do you do?" in English. Context determines if you are asking about their current physical action or their profession.

wat.form_note: question word functioning as the direct object; sits in first position, triggering inversion (verb-second) before the subject
wat.fast_speech: before 'doet', the final /t/ assimilates to /d/ and merges: 'wat doet' sounds like /ʋɑˈdut/

doet.form_note: 3rd person singular (hij/zij) present tense of the irregular verb 'doen'; in an A2 exam answer about an action, you typically replace 'doet' with a specific action verb (e.g., 'De vrouw kookt') rather than repeating 'doet'
doet.fast_speech: before 'de', the final /t/ merges with /d/: 'doet de' sounds like /ˈdudə/

de.form_note: definite article for common-gender (de-word) singular nouns; can be reused in your answer ('De vrouw...') or replaced together with the noun by 'Zij...'

vrouw.form_note: singular common-gender noun (de-word) acting as the subject; in your answer, start with 'De vrouw' or 'Zij' in position 1 followed immediately by the conjugated verb in position 2

sentences.nl: Vertel ook hoe vaak ze dat doet.
sentences.en: Also tell how often she does that.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Vertel (Tell) | ook (also) | hoe vaak (how often) | ze (she) | dat (that) | doet (does).  
• Natural English: "Also tell [me/us] how often she does that."

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Imperative Mood:** *Vertel* is the imperative (command) form of *vertellen* (to tell). It is formed by using the verb stem, with no subject pronoun needed.  
• **Indirect Question Word Order:** The phrase *hoe vaak ze dat doet* is a subordinate clause (an indirect question). In Dutch subordinate clauses, the conjugated verb (*doet*) is pushed to the very end of the sentence.  
• **Extensions:**  
  – *Vraag ook hoe laat hij komt.* (Also ask what time he is coming.)  
  – *Ik weet niet hoe vaak ze traint.* (I don't know how often she works out.)  
  – *Vertel me waarom je dat doet.* (Tell me why you do that.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Laat me weten hoe vaak je naar de sportschool gaat. (Let me know how often you go to the gym.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Using imperatives like *Vertel...* (Tell...) is very normal in Dutch and is not considered rude or overly bossy, especially in instructions, exams, or casual conversation. It reflects the general Dutch preference for direct and efficient communication without unnecessary fluff like "Could you please...".

vertel.form_note: imperative (command form) of 'vertellen' (same form as the ik-present stem). On the A2 speaking exam, 'Vertel...' introduces an indirect question.
vertel.fast_speech: The prefix 'ver-' is unstressed and reduced: /vərˈtɛl/ or /fərˈtɛl/.

ook.form_note: adverb adding a second part to the exam prompt; you do not need to repeat 'ook' in your answer.

hoe.form_note: question word; together with 'vaak' ('hoe vaak' = how often) it introduces a subordinate clause (indirect question) after 'Vertel', pushing the verb 'doet' to the end.

vaak.form_note: adverb of frequency combined with 'hoe' ('hoe vaak' = how often). In your exam answer, replace 'hoe vaak' with a frequency like 'elke dag' or 'twee keer per week'.
vaak.fast_speech: Initial /v/ is often devoiced toward /f/ in the Netherlands: /faːk/.

ze.form_note: unstressed subject pronoun, 3rd person singular feminine (weak form of 'zij'). Because the verb 'doet' is singular, 'ze' here means 'she' (not 'they'). Reuse 'ze' (or 'zij') as the subject of your answer.

dat.form_note: demonstrative pronoun acting as the direct object of 'doet', referring back to the activity mentioned in the first part of the exam prompt.

doet.form_note: 3rd person singular (zij/ze) present tense of irregular verb 'doen'. It stands at the end because 'hoe vaak ze dat doet' is an indirect question after 'Vertel'. When you answer with a normal main clause, move 'doet' to second position (e.g. 'Ze doet dat elke dag').

grammarHits.highlight: Vertel ook hoe vaak ze dat doet
grammarHits.explanation: hoe vaak starts the clause; doet is the last word.

sentences.nl: Ik zie een vrouw.
sentences.en: I see a woman.
sentences.note: Meester's reference answer, built from the topic bank.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **Ik** (I) – **zie** (see) – **een** (a/an) – **vrouw** (woman).  
• Natural English: "I see a woman."

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Word Order (SVO):** Like English, simple main clauses in Dutch follow the Subject-Verb-Object order: *Ik* (Subject) + *zie* (Verb) + *een vrouw* (Object).  
• **Verb Conjugation:** *Zie* is the first-person singular (ik) present tense form of the irregular verb *zien* (to see).  
• **Articles and Gender:** *Een* is the indefinite article ("a" or "an"), which is used for all singular nouns regardless of gender. *Vrouw* is a common-gender noun (a *de*-word), meaning "the woman" would be *de vrouw*.  

**Extensions:**  
• Ik zie een man. (I see a man.)  
• Jij ziet een hond. (You see a dog.)  
• Wij zien de vrouw. (We see the woman.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Ik zie een mooie auto in de straat. (I see a nice car in the street.)  

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch, *vrouw* means both "woman" and "wife." Context usually makes it clear, though *mijn vrouw* always means "my wife." If you are addressing a woman directly (like "ma'am" or "madam"), you do not use *vrouw*; instead, you use the polite form *mevrouw*.

ik.form_note: 1st person singular subject pronoun; starts the main clause in position 1
ik.fast_speech: often unstressed and reduced to /ək/ in connected speech

zie.form_note: 1st person singular (ik) present tense of the irregular verb 'zien'; sits in position 2 (verb-second rule), directly reusing the exam question's verb (e.g. 'Wat zie je?')

een.form_note: indefinite article, used before both singular de-words and het-words (here before the de-word 'vrouw')
een.fast_speech: always pronounced with a short schwa /ən/ when it means 'a' (unlike the number 'één' /eːn/)

vrouw.form_note: singular common gender noun (de-word), acting as the direct object of 'zie'

sentences.nl: Ze poetst haar tanden.
sentences.en: She is brushing her teeth.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Ze = She  
• poetst = brushes / polishes  
• haar = her  
• tanden = teeth  

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Verb Conjugation:** The verb is *poetsen* (to brush/polish). The stem is *poets*. Because the subject is *ze* (third-person singular), we add a **-t** to the stem, making it *poetst*.  
• **Possessive Pronouns with Body Parts:** Similar to English, Dutch uses a possessive pronoun (*haar*, *zijn*, *mijn*) before body parts when talking about daily routines, rather than a reflexive pronoun and a definite article (as is common in German or French).  
• **Extensions:**  
– Ik poets mijn tanden. (I brush my teeth.)  
– Hij wast zijn handen. (He washes his hands.)  
– Ze kamt haar haar. (She combs her hair.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Hij poetst elke avond zijn tanden voor het slapengaan. (He brushes his teeth every evening before going to sleep.)  

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch, the verb *poetsen* is not only used for brushing teeth (*tandenpoetsen*), but also for polishing shoes (*schoenen poetsen*) or general household cleaning/scrubbing (especially in the southern provinces and Belgium).

ze.form_note: unstressed subject pronoun (3rd person singular feminine); stressed form is 'zij'

poetst.form_note: 3rd person singular (zij) present tense of 'poetsen' (stem 'poets' + -t); in the verb-second position of this main clause (also part of the fixed expression 'tanden poetsen')
poetst.fast_speech: the -tst cluster is often simplified to /pust/ or /putst/ with a weak first /t/

haar.form_note: 3rd person singular feminine possessive pronoun, modifying 'tanden'
haar.fast_speech: often reduced to /dər/ ('d'r') in casual speech: 'Ze poetst d'r tanden'

tanden.form_note: plural of tand: add -en; serves as the direct object of 'poetst'
tanden.fast_speech: final -n is usually dropped in standard speech: /ˈtɑndə/

sentences.nl: Ze doet dat twee keer per dag.
sentences.en: She does that twice a day.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Ze = She  
• doet = does  
• dat = that  
• twee = two  
• keer = time(s)  
• per = per / a  
• dag = day  

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Singular "keer":** In Dutch, nouns indicating measurement, time, or frequency (like *keer*, *jaar*, *uur*) remain in the singular form after a number greater than one. Therefore, you say *twee keer* (literally "two time"), not *twee keren*.  
• **Frequency with "per":** The preposition *per* is used just like the English "per" or "a" to express rates and frequencies (e.g., *per dag*, *per week*, *per uur*).  
• **Verb "doen":** *Doet* is the third-person singular present tense of the irregular verb *doen* (to do).  
• **Extensions:**  
– Ik sport drie keer per week. (I work out three times a week.)  
– Hij belt haar één keer per maand. (He calls her once a month.)  
– Wij doen dit elk jaar. (We do this every year.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Ik poets mijn tanden twee keer per dag. (I brush my teeth twice a day.)

ze.form_note: unstressed subject pronoun (3rd person singular feminine); acts as the subject in position 1 of the main clause

doet.form_note: 3rd person singular present tense of the irregular verb 'doen'; placed in the verb-second (V2) position right after the subject, reusing the verb from a 'Wat doet ze...?' exam question

sentences.nl: Dit zijn Megan en Koen.
sentences.en: These are Megan and Koen.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Dit (This) zijn (are) Megan (Megan) en (and) Koen (Koen).  
*(Natural English: "These are Megan and Koen.")*

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Singular "Dit" with Plural Nouns:** In English, you must switch from "this" to "these" for plural nouns ("These are..."). In Dutch, when introducing people or things, you keep the singular neuter pronoun **dit** (this) or **dat** (that), even when followed by the plural verb **zijn** (are) and plural subjects.  
• **Zijn:** This is the present plural form of the verb *zijn* (to be), matching the plural subject (Megan and Koen).  

**Extensions:**  
• Dit zijn mijn ouders. (These are my parents.)  
• Dat zijn de nieuwe buren. (Those are the new neighbors.)  
• Dit zijn mijn boeken. (These are my books.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Dit zijn mijn goede vrienden, Lisa en Mark. (These are my good friends, Lisa and Mark.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• **Koen** is a classic, very common Dutch male name (short for Koenraad). Meanwhile, English names like **Megan** have become increasingly popular in the Netherlands over the last few decades. When being introduced to two people like this in a casual Dutch setting, it is standard to shake hands with both and say your own first name, or simply say a general *"Hoi"* or *"Leuk je te ontmoeten"* (Nice to meet you).

dit.form_note: In Dutch, singular 'dit' is used as the introductory subject even when introducing plural people or things ('Dit zijn...' = 'These are...').

zijn.form_note: present tense plural (3rd person plural) of the irregular verb 'zijn'; agrees in number with 'Megan en Koen' and sits in the second position (verb-second rule).
zijn.fast_speech: often unstressed and reduced to /zən/ in casual speech

megan.form_note: proper name, part of the plural predicate ('Megan en Koen') which makes the verb plural.

en.form_note: links the two proper nouns 'Megan' and 'Koen'.
en.fast_speech: often reduced to /ən/ or /n/

koen.form_note: Dutch male proper name, second part of the plural predicate.

sentences.nl: Vertel wat over Megan en Koen.
sentences.en: Tell something about Megan and Koen.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Vertel (Tell) – wat (something / a bit) – over (about) – Megan (Megan) – en (and) – Koen (Koen).  
• Natural translation: "Tell [me] something about Megan and Koen."

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Imperative Mood (Gebiedende wijs):** The sentence starts with *Vertel*, which is the stem of the verb *vertellen* (to tell). Placing the verb stem at the very beginning of the sentence without a subject turns it into a command or request.  
• **Use of "wat":** While *wat* usually means "what," in spoken and informal Dutch it is very frequently used as an indefinite pronoun meaning *iets* (something) or *een beetje* (a little bit).  
• **Preposition:** *Vertellen* pairs with the preposition *over* to mean "to tell about."

• **Extensions:**  
– *Vertel eens wat over jezelf.* (Tell [me] something about yourself.)  
– *Ik weet al wat over dat project.* (I already know a bit about that project.)  
– *Zeg wat over zijn nieuwe boek.* (Say something about his new book.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Vertel wat over je vakantie in Spanje. (Tell me something about your vacation in Spain.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• **Dutch Directness & Particles:** A bare imperative like *Vertel wat...* can sometimes sound a bit abrupt in Dutch. In daily conversation, native speakers almost always soften commands by adding modal particles like **eens** or **maar** right after the verb (e.g., *Vertel **eens** wat over Megan en Koen*). This makes it sound like a friendly invitation to chat rather than a strict order.  
• **Names:** *Koen* (pronounced like "coon") is a classic, very common Dutch male name, originally a short form of *Koenraad* (Conrad).

vertel.form_note: imperative (command form) singular of vertellen, identical to the 1st person singular present stem; in the A2 speaking exam, prompts often start with 'Vertel' instead of a direct question, so you can answer with a normal main clause (e.g. 'Megan en Koen zijn...') or an indirect clause
vertel.fast_speech: the unstressed prefix 'ver-' is reduced to /vər/ or /fər/

wat.form_note: used here as an informal indefinite pronoun meaning 'iets' (something), not as the question word 'what'; it functions as the direct object of 'vertel'

over.form_note: preposition paired with the verb 'vertellen' (vertellen over = to tell about) to introduce the topic; you can reuse 'over' in your answer or make the topic your subject

megan.form_note: proper noun (first name), part of the prepositional object after 'over'

en.form_note: coordinating conjunction linking the two proper nouns 'Megan' and 'Koen' into a plural group (if you make them the subject of your answer, use the plural verb form)
en.fast_speech: often reduced to /ən/ in connected speech

koen.form_note: proper noun (Dutch male first name), part of the prepositional object after 'over'

sentences.nl: Noem drie dingen.
sentences.en: Name three things.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Noem (Name / Mention) drie (three) dingen (things).  
• Natural translation: "Name three things."

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Imperative Mood:** *Noem* is the stem of the verb *noemen* (to name, to mention, or to call). In Dutch, commands or instructions are formed by placing the verb stem at the very beginning of the sentence, without a subject pronoun.  
• **Plural Nouns:** *Dingen* is the plural form of *het ding* (the thing). Adding *-en* is the most common way to make a noun plural in Dutch.  
• **Extensions:**  
  – *Noem een voorbeeld.* (Name an example.)  
  – *Ik heb drie boeken.* (I have three books.)  
  – *Hoe noem je dat?* (What do you call that?)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Noem twee goede redenen om te blijven. (Name two good reasons to stay.)

noem.form_note: imperative (command form) of the verb 'noemen' (uses the verb stem, which is the 'ik'-form in the present tense). In the A2 speaking exam, this is a prompt to give a list instead of reusing the verb.

drie.form_note: cardinal number; specifies how many examples you must give for your exam answer to be complete

sentences.nl: Gebruik het plaatje.
sentences.en: Use the picture.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Gebruik (Use)  
• het (the)  
• plaatje. (little picture / image.)  

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **The Imperative (De Gebiedende Wijs):** The sentence starts with *Gebruik*, which is the command form of the verb *gebruiken* (to use). In Dutch, the informal singular imperative is simply the verb stem (the *ik*-form) placed at the very beginning of the sentence, with no subject pronoun.  
• **Diminutive Noun (Verkleinwoord):** *Plaatje* is the diminutive form of *de plaat* (plate/sheet/large picture). Adding the suffix *-je* makes it mean "small picture," "illustration," or "image." Crucially, **all** diminutive nouns in Dutch are neuter and take the definite article *het*, regardless of the original noun's gender.  
• **Extensions:**  
  – *Gebruik een potlood.* (Use a pencil.)  
  – *Kijk naar het plaatje.* (Look at the picture.)  
  – *Lees het boekje.* (Read the booklet/little book.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Gebruik het woordenboekje als je een woord niet kent. (Use the little dictionary if you don't know a word.)  

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• While *plaatje* literally means "small picture," it is the standard everyday Dutch word for illustrations in textbooks, icons on a computer screen, or collectible trading cards/stickers. In the Netherlands, supermarkets often run wildly popular campaigns where shoppers collect *plaatjes* (like football players or nature stickers to paste into an album) with their groceries.

gebruik.form_note: imperative (command form) of gebruiken, identical to the 1st-person singular present stem; placed first to give an instruction in the speaking exam

het.form_note: neuter singular definite article; all Dutch diminutive nouns (ending in -je) take 'het'
het.fast_speech: usually unstressed and pronounced /ət/

plaatje.form_note: singular diminutive of de plaat (plate/print/record), formed by adding -je; here it is the direct object of 'gebruik'

sentences.nl: Ze hangen samen de bruine gordijnen in hun nieuwe huis op.
sentences.en: Together they are hanging up the brown curtains in their new house.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **Ze** (They) **hangen** (hang) **samen** (together) **de bruine gordijnen** (the brown curtains) **in hun nieuwe huis** (in their new house) **op** (up).  
• Natural English: They are hanging up the brown curtains together in their new house.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Separable Verb (*ophangen*):** The verb *ophangen* (to hang up) splits in the present tense main clause. The main verb (*hangen*) takes the second position, and the prefix (*op*) goes all the way to the end of the sentence, creating a "sentence bracket."  
• **Adjective Endings (*bruine* / *nieuwe*):** Both *bruin* and *nieuw* get an *-e* ending. *Gordijnen* is plural, and although *huis* is a *het*-word, the possessive pronoun *hun* (their) makes the noun definite, which triggers the *-e* ending on the adjective.  
• **Extensions:**  
– Ik **hang** mijn natte jas **op**. (I hang up my wet coat.)  
– Wij koken **samen** in **ons nieuwe huis**. (We cook together in our new house.)  
– Zij doet **de groene gordijnen** dicht. (She closes the green curtains.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Wij hangen morgen de grote schilderijen in onze kleine woonkamer op. (We are hanging up the big paintings in our small living room tomorrow.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• While you are hanging curtains here, you might notice that many Dutch people keep their living room curtains wide open, even at night with the lights on. Rooted in Calvinist history, this tradition stems from the idea that "if you behave well, you have nothing to hide." However, it is considered polite for passersby not to stare directly inside!

ze.form_note: unstressed subject pronoun, 3rd person plural (known to be plural here because the verb 'hangen' is plural)

hangen.form_note: 3rd person plural present tense of the separable verb 'ophangen' (to hang up); the verb stem is in the second position (V2) and the prefix 'op' is at the end of the clause

samen.form_note: adverb of manner placed right after the finite verb

de.form_note: definite article used for all plural nouns (even though singular 'het gordijn' is a het-word)

bruine.form_note: inflected with -e because it precedes a plural noun ('gordijnen')

gordijnen.form_note: plural of 'het gordijn': regular plural formed by adding -en

in.form_note: preposition introducing the location phrase 'in hun nieuwe huis'

hun.form_note: possessive determiner, 3rd person plural; makes the noun phrase definite
hun.fast_speech: initial /ɦ/ is often weak in connected speech after 'in'

nieuwe.form_note: inflected with -e because even though 'huis' is a singular het-word, it is preceded by a possessive determiner ('hun'), which makes it definite

op.form_note: separated prefix of the separable verb 'ophangen' (hangen ... op), placed at the very end of the main clause

sentences.nl: Megan en Koen zijn in de woonkamer.
sentences.en: Megan and Koen are in the living room.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Megan – Megan  
• en – and  
• Koen – Koen  
• zijn – are  
• in – in  
• de – the  
• woonkamer – living room (literally: live-room)  

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Subject-Verb Agreement:** Because the subject is plural (*Megan en Koen*), the irregular verb *zijn* (to be) takes the plural present tense form, which is also *zijn* (are).  
• **Gender and Articles:** *Woonkamer* is a compound noun (*wonen* + *kamer*). In Dutch, compound nouns take the gender of the last word. Since *kamer* is a common gender noun (*de*-word), it is *de woonkamer*.  
• **Standard Word Order:** This sentence follows the basic Subject – Verb – Place (SVP) order.  

**Extensions:**  
• De kinderen zijn in de tuin. (The children are in the garden.)  
• Mijn ouders zijn in de keuken. (My parents are in the kitchen.)  
• De stoel en de tafel zijn in de woonkamer. (The chair and the table are in the living room.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Sem en Sophie zijn in de slaapkamer. (Sem and Sophie are in the bedroom.)  

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• **Koen:** This is a very common traditional Dutch male name, originally a short form of *Koenraad* (Conrad).  
• **De woonkamer:** In traditional Dutch houses, the *woonkamer* typically has very large windows facing the street. Culturally, many Dutch people leave their curtains open in the evening, stemming from a tradition of having "nothing to hide," though it is polite for passersby not to stare directly inside.

megan.form_note: part of the compound subject 'Megan en Koen'

en.form_note: coordinating conjunction joining the two names into a plural subject
en.fast_speech: often reduced to /ən/ or /n/ between words

koen.form_note: part of the compound subject 'Megan en Koen'

zijn.form_note: 3rd person plural present tense of the irregular verb 'zijn' (to be); sits in second position (V2) right after the compound subject 'Megan en Koen'

in.form_note: preposition of place introducing the location 'in de woonkamer'

de.form_note: definite article for singular common-gender (de-) nouns like 'woonkamer'

woonkamer.form_note: singular compound de-noun made from 'woon' (verb stem of 'wonen', to live) + 'kamer' (room)

sentences.nl: Koen houdt de trap vast, want Megan wil de gordijnen wassen.
sentences.en: Koen is holding the stepladder, because Megan wants to wash the curtains.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Koen = Koen  
• houdt = holds  
• de trap = the stairs / the ladder  
• vast = fast / tight (part of the verb *vasthouden*, "to hold on to")  
• want = because / for  
• Megan = Megan  
• wil = wants  
• de gordijnen = the curtains  
• wassen = to wash  
• *Natural translation: Koen holds the ladder steady, because Megan wants to wash the curtains.*

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Separable Verb (*vasthouden*):** The verb *vasthouden* (to hold tight/steady) splits in the present tense. The stem (*houdt*) takes the second position, and the prefix (*vast*) goes to the end of that specific clause.  
• **Coordinating Conjunction (*want*):** *Want* means "because." Unlike *omdat* (which pushes the verb to the end), *want* does not change the word order of the second clause. It remains Subject (*Megan*) + Verb (*wil*).  
• **Modal Verb (*willen*):** *Wil* (wants) is a modal verb. It stays in the second position of its clause, and the action verb it modifies (*wassen*) is pushed to the very end in its infinitive form.  
• **Extensions:**  
  – Houd mijn hand vast, want de straat is glad. (Hold my hand tight, because the street is slippery.)  
  – Ik blijf vandaag thuis, want ik wil mijn kleren wassen. (I am staying home today, because I want to wash my clothes.)  
  – Hij zet de deur open, want de hond wil naar buiten. (He props the door open, because the dog wants to go outside.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Sander houdt de doos vast, want hij wil zijn kamer opruimen. (Sander holds the box, because he wants to tidy up his room.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• **Trap vs. Ladder:** In Dutch, *de trap* usually means "the stairs." However, in the context of household chores, *een trap* (or the diminutive *een trapje*) refers to a freestanding A-frame stepladder.  
• **Dutch Windows:** Historically and culturally, the Dutch are famous for keeping their windows and curtains spotless, often leaving the curtains wide open during the day to show they have "nothing to hide" (a remnant of Calvinist tradition).

koen.form_note: subject of the first main clause

houdt.form_note: 3rd person singular present tense of the separable verb 'vasthouden' (to hold on to / to steady); stem 'houd' + -t, placed in second position while the prefix 'vast' goes to the end of the clause
houdt.fast_speech: The 'dt' is pronounced as a single /t/ sound.

de.form_note: plural definite article (all plural nouns take 'de' in Dutch, even though singular 'het gordijn' is a het-word)

trap.form_note: singular common-gender noun ('de trap'), direct object of 'vasthouden'

vast.form_note: separated prefix of 'vasthouden' ('houdt ... vast'), placed at the end of the first main clause

want.form_note: connects two main clauses; unlike 'omdat', 'want' keeps normal main-clause word order (subject + conjugated verb in second position)

megan.form_note: subject of the second main clause after 'want'

wil.form_note: 3rd person singular present tense of the modal verb 'willen'; irregular because hij/zij form takes no -t ('wil', not 'wilt'); stands in second position of the 'want' clause and sends the infinitive 'wassen' to the end

gordijnen.form_note: plural of 'het gordijn': add -en; direct object of 'wassen'

wassen.form_note: infinitive of 'wassen', placed at the very end of the clause because of the modal verb 'wil'

sentences.nl: Ik zie een man en een vrouw.
sentences.en: I see a man and a woman.
sentences.note: Meester's reference answer, built from the topic bank.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Ik (I) – zie (see) – een (a) – man (man) – en (and) – een (a) – vrouw (woman).  
• Natural English: "I see a man and a woman."

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Word Order (SVO):** Like English, basic Dutch declarative sentences follow the Subject-Verb-Object order. Here, *Ik* is the subject, *zie* is the verb, and *een man en een vrouw* is the direct object.
• **Verb Conjugation:** *Zie* is the first-person singular (ik) present tense form of the irregular verb *zien* (to see). 
• **Indefinite Article:** *Een* means "a" or "an". Unlike the definite articles (*de* and *het*), *een* is used for all singular nouns regardless of their grammatical gender. (Note: It is pronounced with a short, unstressed "uh" sound, unlike the number *één* which means "one").

• **Extensions:**  
  – Ik zie een hond en een kat. (I see a dog and a cat.)  
  – Jij ziet een man. (You see a man.)  
  – De man en de vrouw zien mij. (The man and the woman see me.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Ik zie een jongen en een meisje op straat. (I see a boy and a girl on the street.)

ik.form_note: first-person singular subject pronoun; starts the main clause in position 1
ik.fast_speech: often unstressed and reduced to /ək/ in connected speech

zie.form_note: first-person singular (ik) present tense of the irregular verb 'zien'; stands in the verb-second (V2) position, reusing the verb from an exam question like 'Wat zie je op het plaatje?'

een.form_note: indefinite article used before singular countable nouns of either gender (de or het); modifies 'vrouw'
een.fast_speech: always pronounced with a schwa /ən/, not like the number 'één' (/eːn/)

man.form_note: singular common-gender (de) noun; part of the direct object of 'zie'

en.form_note: coordinating conjunction connecting the two direct objects 'een man' and 'een vrouw'
en.fast_speech: often reduced to /ən/ or /n/ in fast speech

vrouw.form_note: singular common-gender (de) noun; part of the direct object of 'zie'

sentences.nl: Ze hangen de gordijnen op.
sentences.en: They are hanging up the curtains.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Ze – They  
• hangen – hang  
• de gordijnen – the curtains  
• op – up  
• (Natural translation: They are hanging up the curtains.)

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Separable Verb (*scheidbaar werkwoord*):** The verb here is *ophangen* (to hang up). In a main clause in the present tense, the verb splits: the stem (*hangen*) goes to the second position, and the prefix (*op*) is kicked to the very end of the sentence.  
• **Pronoun *Ze*:** *Ze* can mean "she" or "they". Because the verb *hangen* is plural, we know *ze* means "they" in this sentence (if it were "she", it would be *Ze hangt...*).  
• **Plural Nouns:** *Gordijnen* is the plural of *het gordijn*. All plural nouns in Dutch take the article *de*, even if the singular noun is a *het*-word.  

• **Extensions:**  
– Ik hang mijn jas op. (I hang up my coat.)  
– Kun je de was ophangen? (Can you hang up the laundry? — *Note: the verb stays together at the end because of the modal verb 'kun'*.)  
– Hij doet de gordijnen dicht. (He closes the curtains — *using the separable verb 'dichtdoen'*.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Wij hangen het nieuwe schilderij in de woonkamer op. (We are hanging up the new painting in the living room.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, you might notice that many people hang curtains (*gordijnen*) or sheer curtains (*vitrages*) but rarely close them completely, even at night. This stems from a cultural tradition of openness (often attributed to Calvinist roots) showing that one has "nothing to hide." Looking directly inside as you walk by, however, is still considered impolite!

ze.form_note: unstressed subject pronoun (3rd person plural, because the verb 'hangen' is plural). Acts as the subject in position 1.

hangen.form_note: 3rd person plural present tense of the separable verb 'ophangen' (to hang up). In a main clause, the conjugated stem 'hangen' sits in position 2 (verb-second rule) and the prefix 'op' goes to the end.

de.form_note: definite article used before plural nouns. Although singular 'het gordijn' is a het-word, ALL plural nouns in Dutch take 'de'.

gordijnen.form_note: plural of gordijn: add -en. Acts as the direct object of the sentence.

op.form_note: separable prefix of the verb 'ophangen'. In a main clause in the present tense, the prefix separates from the verb and goes to the very end of the sentence.

grammarHits.explanation: ophangen splits: hangen in second place, op at the end.

sentences.nl: Megan staat op een trap en Koen helpt haar.
sentences.en: Megan is standing on a stepladder and Koen is helping her.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Megan – Megan  
• staat – stands / is standing  
• op – on  
• een – a  
• trap – stairs / stepladder  
• en – and  
• Koen – Koen  
• helpt – helps / is helping  
• haar – her  

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Coordinating Conjunction (en):** The word *en* (and) connects two independent clauses. It does not change the standard word order, so both parts follow the basic Subject–Verb–Object/Preposition pattern (*Megan staat...* and *Koen helpt...*).  
• **Posture Verb (staan):** Dutch prefers specific posture verbs (*staan* - to stand, *zitten* - to sit, *liggen* - to lie) to indicate where someone or something is, whereas English often just uses "to be" (e.g., "Megan is on the stairs").  
• **Present Tense:** Both *staat* (from *staan*) and *helpt* (from *helpen*) are third-person singular present tense verbs, formed by taking the verb stem and adding **-t**.  
• **Vocabulary Note:** The word *trap* can mean both a regular flight of stairs and a freestanding stepladder (often called a *trapje* or *keukentrap*).  

**Extensions:**  
• De kat zit op de trap. (The cat is sitting on the stairs.)  
• Hij staat op de tafel en zij kijkt naar hem. (He is standing on the table and she is looking at him.)  
• Ik zoek mijn sleutels en mijn broer helpt mij. (I am looking for my keys and my brother is helping me.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Sara staat op een stoel en Thomas geeft haar een boek. (Sara is standing on a chair and Thomas is giving her a book.)  

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Traditional Dutch houses, especially historic canal houses in cities like Amsterdam, are famous for having extremely steep and narrow staircases (*trappen*). Because of this, moving large furniture up the stairs is often impossible; instead, the Dutch use a *verhuislift* (moving lift) outside the window or the traditional hoisting beam (*hijsbalk*) attached to the top of the house's facade.

sentences.nl: U volgt een opleiding.
sentences.en: You are taking a course.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• U (You [formal])  
• volgt (follow / are following)  
• een (a / an)  
• opleiding (training / education program / course of study).  
*(Natural translation: You are taking a training program / You are studying a course.)*

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Collocation:** In Dutch, you do not "take" or "do" an education program; you "follow" it (*een opleiding volgen*). This also applies to classes, courses, and lectures.  
• **Formal Pronoun (*U*):** *U* is the polite/formal way to say "you" (both singular and plural). For regular verbs in the present tense, *u* always takes the stem + t (*volg* + *t* = *volgt*).  
• **Present Tense Usage:** Dutch uses the simple present (*volgt*) to express both a general fact ("You follow") and an ongoing action ("You are following").  

**Extensions:**  
• Zij volgt een cursus Nederlands. (She is taking a Dutch course.)  
• Welke opleiding volg je? (Which study program are you following? [informal])  
• Wij volgen morgen een workshop. (We are attending a workshop tomorrow.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Mijn broer volgt een opleiding tot timmerman. (My brother is doing a training program to become a carpenter.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, the word *opleiding* is used very broadly for any structured path toward a diploma or certificate—whether it is a vocational trade (MBO), a university degree (HBO/WO), or professional job training. Because the sentence uses the formal *U*, you will often see or hear this exact phrase in official contexts, such as on government websites (like DUO, which handles student finance), tax forms, or during job interviews.

u.form_note: formal subject pronoun (2nd person singular and plural); in an A2 exam prompt, the examiner uses 'u' to address you, and when you answer, you change 'u' to 'ik'

volgt.form_note: present tense of 'volgen' for 'u' (stem 'volg' + -t), placed in the second position of the main clause; to answer the exam question, reuse this verb in the 'ik' form: 'Ik volg...'

een.form_note: indefinite article used before singular nouns (both de- and het-words)
een.fast_speech: Always pronounced with a short, unstressed schwa /ən/, unlike the number 'één' (one) which is /eːn/.

opleiding.form_note: singular de-word functioning as the direct object; the collocation 'een opleiding volgen' means to take a course or study a program

sentences.nl: In welk gebouw hebt u liever les?
sentences.en: In which building would you rather have class?
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• In = In  
• welk = which  
• gebouw = building  
• hebt = have  
• u = you (formal)  
• liever = rather / preferably  
• les? = lesson / class?  

*(Natural translation: In which building would you rather have class?)*

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Welk vs. Welke:** The word for "which" changes based on the noun's gender. Because *gebouw* is a neuter noun (*het gebouw*), it uses *welk* (without an -e) in the singular form. Common gender nouns (*de*-words) and all plural nouns use *welke*.  
• **Word Order (Inversion):** Because the question starts with a prepositional phrase (*In welk gebouw*), the verb (*hebt*) must come immediately second, followed by the subject (*u*).  
• **Hebben + liever:** Combining a verb with *liever* is the standard Dutch way to express "to prefer [doing something]" or "would rather."  
• **Les hebben:** Literally "to have lesson," this is a fixed expression meaning to have class or to be taught.  

**Extensions:**  
• Op welke dag hebt u liever een afspraak? (On which day would you rather have an appointment?)  
• Welk boek leest u liever? (Which book do you prefer reading?)  
• Zij heeft vandaag geen les. (She doesn't have class today.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• In welk lokaal werken de studenten liever aan hun project? (In which classroom do the students prefer to work on their project?)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• **Hebt u vs. Heeft u:** Both *hebt u* and *heeft u* are grammatically correct for the formal "you have." *Heeft u* is slightly more common and considered a bit more polished in the Randstad (the western urban area of the Netherlands), while *hebt u* is used frequently in the south, in Belgium (Flanders), and in written guidelines, as it directly mirrors the informal *jij hebt*.
