sentences.nl: Vertel ook waarom.
sentences.en: Also tell why.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Vertel (Tell) – ook (also) – waarom (why).  
• Natural translation: Also tell (us/me) why. / Explain why as well.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Imperative Mood (De gebiedende wijs):** The sentence starts with *Vertel*, which is the stem of the verb *vertellen* (to tell/narrate). Starting a sentence with the verb stem and omitting the subject creates a direct command or instruction.  
• **Verb Difference (*Vertellen* vs. *Zeggen*):** Dutch uses *vertellen* when asking for a story, explanation, or longer details, whereas *zeggen* is used for simply stating words or facts.  
• **Adverb Placement:** The adverb *ook* (also/too) is placed immediately after the imperative verb to add the instruction onto a previous one.  
• **Extensions:**  
  – *Leg ook uit hoe.* (Also explain how.)  
  – *Vertel eens wat er is gebeurd.* (Tell me what happened.)  
  – *Schrijf ook op waar je woont.* (Also write down where you live.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Kies je favoriete boek en vertel ook waarom je het goed vindt. (Choose your favorite book and also tell us why you like it.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• This exact phrase is classic Dutch "school language" (*schooltaal*). You will see it constantly on Dutch exams, in textbooks, and on civic integration tests (*inburgeringsexamen*). Because the Dutch culture and education system heavily value directness, critical thinking, and substantiating your opinions, a simple "yes" or "no" is rarely enough—you are almost always expected to motivate your answer.

vertel.form_note: imperative (command form) of 'vertellen', equal to the stem (ik-form). Placed first in the sentence to give an instruction. In the A2 speaking exam, you answer this prompt using 'want' + a main clause (verb-second).

ook.form_note: invariable adverb; placed directly after the imperative verb to add an extra task to the previous exam question

waarom.form_note: interrogative adverb functioning here as a shortened indirect question (object of 'vertel'). In your exam answer, replace 'waarom' with 'want' (because) followed by a main clause with the verb in second position.
waarom.fast_speech: first vowel is often shortened in connected speech: /ʋɑˈrɔm/

sentences.nl: Kies één van de plaatjes.
sentences.en: Choose one of the pictures.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Kies – Choose  
• één – one  
• van – of  
• de – the  
• plaatjes – little pictures  

(Natural English: Choose one of the pictures.)

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Imperative Mood:** *Kies* is the imperative (command) form of the verb *kiezen* (to choose). To form a command in Dutch, you simply use the verb stem (the *ik*-form) at the very beginning of the sentence without a subject.  
• **Accent Marks for Emphasis:** Notice the accents on *één*. Unaccented *een* means "a/an" (unstressed), while accented *één* specifically means the number "one" (stressed).  
• **Diminutive Noun:** *Plaatjes* is the plural diminutive of *de plaat* (plate/large print). Adding *-je(s)* makes it small, turning the meaning into standard "pictures", "illustrations", or "images".

**Extensions:**  
• *Kies een nummer tussen één en tien.* (Choose a number between one and ten.)  
• *Pak één van de koekjes.* (Take one of the cookies.)  
• *Dit boek heeft mooie plaatjes.* (This book has nice pictures.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• *Lees één van de korte verhaaltjes.* (Read one of the short stories.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• **Football Stickers (*Voetbalplaatjes*):** While *een foto* is a photograph and *een schilderij* is a painting, *een plaatje* usually refers to a printed image or illustration. In the Netherlands, collecting *plaatjes* (specifically *voetbalplaatjes*—football player stickers/cards) from supermarkets like Albert Heijn during major tournaments is a massive cultural craze among both children and adults.

kies.form_note: imperative singular of kiezen (uses the ik-form; z becomes s at the end of a syllable). To answer this exam prompt, start with 'Ik kies...' followed by the picture you want.

één.form_note: written with accent marks (één) to stress the number 'one' and distinguish it from the unstressed indefinite article 'een' (a/an).

van.fast_speech: initial /v/ is often pronounced closer to /f/ (/fɑn/)

de.form_note: plural definite article; all plural nouns in Dutch take 'de', even when the singular is a 'het'-word like 'het plaatje'.

plaatjes.form_note: plural of het plaatje (diminutive of de plaat): add -s (all diminutives ending in -je form their plural by adding -s).

sentences.nl: In het oude gebouw, want dat vind ik mooier.
sentences.en: In the old building, because I think that one is nicer.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• In – In  
• het – the  
• oude – old  
• gebouw, – building,  
• want – because / for  
• dat – that (one)  
• vind – find (think)  
• ik – I  
• mooier. – prettier / more beautiful.  

(Natural English: "In the old building, because I like that one better / find that one prettier.")

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Adjective inflection ("het oude gebouw"):** Even though *gebouw* is a *het*-word, the adjective *oud* gets an **-e** ending (*oude*) because it is preceded by the definite article *het*. (Compare with the indefinite: *een oud gebouw*).  
• **Coordinating conjunction ("want"):** *Want* means "because" and connects two main clauses. Unlike *omdat* (which pushes the verb to the end), *want* does not change the standard word order of the clause that follows.  
• **Topicalization & Inversion ("dat vind ik"):** Instead of starting the second clause with the subject (*ik vind dat*), the object *dat* (referring back to *het gebouw*) is placed first for emphasis. Because the verb (*vind*) must stay in the second position of the clause, the subject (*ik*) is inverted and placed after the verb.  
• **Expressing opinions with "vinden":** Dutch uses the verb *vinden* (literally "to find") to express personal opinions, equivalent to "I think" or "I like [something] [comparative]" in English.  

**Extensions:**  
• Op de nieuwe fiets, want die vind ik sneller. (On the new bike, because I find that one faster. *Note: "die" is used instead of "dat" because "fiets" is a de-word.*)  
• In het kleine huis, want dat vinden wij gezelliger. (In the small house, because we find that one cozier.)  
• Met de blauwe pen, want die vind ik fijner. (With the blue pen, because I like that one better / find it nicer to use.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Aan de grote tafel, want die vind ik handiger.  
(At the big table, because I find that one more convenient.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, historical architecture (*oude gebouwen*, like canal houses or repurposed old factories) is highly prized for its charm and *gezelligheid* (coziness/atmosphere). When choosing a café, office space, or apartment, Dutch people will very commonly favor an older building over a modern one strictly for its aesthetic character, despite older buildings often being less practical or more drafty.

sentences.nl: Ik heb liever les in het moderne gebouw.
sentences.en: I would rather have class in the modern building.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **Ik** (I) **heb** (have) **liever** (rather / preferably) **les** (lesson / class) **in** (in) **het** (the) **moderne** (modern) **gebouw** (building).  
• *Natural translation: I prefer to have class in the modern building.*

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Expressing preference with *liever*:** In Dutch, the adverb *liever* (the comparative form of *graag*) is used with a verb to mean "prefer to [verb]" or "would rather [verb]". Instead of using a separate verb for "prefer," you just add *liever* after the conjugated verb.  
• **The collocation *les hebben*:** Literally "to have lesson," this is the standard Dutch way to say "to have class" or "to be in class."  
• **Adjective inflection:** *Gebouw* is a *het*-word (neuter). Because it is preceded by the definite article *het*, the adjective *modern* takes an **-e** ending (*het moderne gebouw*). If it were indefinite (*een*), it would not take an -e (*een modern gebouw*).

• **Extensions:**  
– Ik drink liever koffie dan thee. (I prefer to drink coffee rather than tea.)  
– Wij hebben morgen geen les. (We don't have class tomorrow.)  
– Zij werkt in dat oude gebouw. (She works in that old building.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Ik werk liever in het rustige kantoor. (I prefer to work in the quiet office.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Many Dutch universities (like the University of Amsterdam or Utrecht University) are integrated into the city center rather than confined to a single campus. Because of this, students frequently travel between historic, centuries-old canal houses and ultra-modern campus buildings on the outskirts for their classes, often having strong preferences for one over the other due to facilities like air conditioning or better Wi-Fi.

sentences.nl: Daar is alles nieuw.
sentences.en: Everything is new there.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Daar = There  
• is = is  
• alles = everything  
• nieuw = new  
*(Natural translation: Everything is new there.)*

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **V2 Word Order and Inversion:** In Dutch main clauses, the conjugated verb (*is*) must always be in the second position. Because this sentence starts with a location word (*Daar*) instead of the subject, the subject (*alles*) gets pushed to the position right after the verb. This is called inversion.  
• **Singular "Alles":** Just like "everything" in English, the pronoun *alles* is grammatically singular, so it takes the singular verb *is* (from *zijn* - to be).  
• **Extensions:**  
– Hier is alles duur. (Everything is expensive here.)  
– Vandaag is alles gesloten. (Today everything is closed.)  
– Thuis is alles rustig. (At home, everything is quiet.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• In die winkel is alles goedkoop. (Everything is cheap in that store.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• *None.*

sentences.nl: Ik kies het tweede plaatje.
sentences.en: I choose the second picture.
sentences.note: Meester's reference answer, built from the topic bank.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Ik (I) kies (choose) het (the) tweede (second) plaatje (little-picture).  
• Natural translation: I choose the second picture.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Verb conjugation:** *Kies* is the first-person singular present tense of the strong verb *kiezen* (to choose).  
• **Diminutive and Gender:** *Plaatje* is the diminutive form of *de plaat* (plate/print/record). In Dutch, all diminutive nouns ending in *-je* change their grammatical gender to neuter, which is why it uses the definite article *het* instead of *de*. (In everyday speech, *plaatje* is the standard word for a small picture, image, or illustration).  
• **Ordinal numbers:** *Tweede* (second) is an ordinal number created by adding *-de* to the cardinal number *twee* (two). Like adjectives, ordinal numbers always end in *-e* when placed after a definite article (*de* or *het*).  
• **Extensions:**  
  – Jij kiest de eerste optie. (You choose the first option.)  
  – Wij bekijken het mooie plaatje. (We look at the pretty picture.)  
  – Zij leest het derde boek. (She reads the third book.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Hij kiest het laatste koekje uit de trommel. (He chooses the last cookie from the tin.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, supermarkets frequently run promotional campaigns where shoppers collect *plaatjes* (stickers or trading cards) to paste into an album—most famously the nature albums written by biologist Freek Vonk at Albert Heijn, or local football club albums. Trading and choosing specific *plaatjes* is a very nostalgic and ongoing part of Dutch daily life for both kids and adults.

• Ik (I) heb (have) liever (rather/preferably) les (lesson/class) in (in) het (the) moderne (modern) gebouw (building),

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Liever (Expressing Preference):** The word *liever* is the comparative form of *graag* (gladly). In Dutch, instead of using a separate verb like "to prefer", you simply add *liever* to the main verb to mean "would rather".  
• **Les hebben:** Literally "to have lesson", this is the standard Dutch idiom for having/attending a class (notice there is no article like *een* before *les*).

• Ik drink **liever** thee dan koffie. (I would rather drink tea than coffee / I prefer tea over coffee.)

• In the Netherlands, universities (like those in Amsterdam, Utrecht, or Leiden) aren't usually isolated campuses; they are spread out across the city. Students often have to cycle between historic, drafty canal houses and brand-new, high-tech facilities (*het moderne gebouw*) on the edge of town for different classes on the same day.

sentences.nl: want het is nieuw en licht.
sentences.en: because it is new and bright.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• want = because / for  
• het = it  
• is = is  
• nieuw = new  
• en = and  
• licht = light (in weight or color/brightness)  
• Natural translation: "...because it is new and light."

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Coordinating Conjunction (*want*):** In Dutch, both *want* and *omdat* mean "because." However, *want* is a coordinating conjunction, meaning it does **not** change the word order of the clause that follows it—the verb (*is*) stays in the normal second position (after the subject *het*).  
• **Predicative Adjectives:** When adjectives like *nieuw* and *licht* come after a linking verb (like *zijn* - to be) and are not directly in front of a noun, they never take an *-e* ending.  
• **Extensions:**  
– Ik koop het niet, want het is oud en zwaar. (I am not buying it, because it is old and heavy.)  
– Hij blijft thuis, want hij is moe. (He is staying home, because he is tired.)  
– Het huis is groot en licht. (The house is big and bright.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Ik neem deze fiets, want hij is snel en licht. (I am taking this bike, because it is fast and light.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• When describing houses or apartments in the Netherlands, the word *licht* (bright/light-filled) is one of the most positive and sought-after traits. Because Dutch winters are long and gray, traditional and modern Dutch architecture alike prioritize huge windows to make the living space as *licht* as possible.

sentences.nl: U zoekt werk in een winkel.
sentences.en: You are looking for work in a shop.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **U** (You - formal) **zoekt** (look for / seek) **werk** (work) **in** (in) **een** (a) **winkel** (shop / store).

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Formal Pronoun (*U*):** *U* is the polite/formal way to say "you" in Dutch. In the present tense, the verb conjugation for *u* is the same as the third-person singular (stem + t). Thus, the verb *zoeken* (to look for) becomes *zoekt*.
• **No Preposition Needed for *Zoeken*:** In English, you say "look *for*", which requires a preposition. In Dutch, the "for" is already built into the verb *zoeken*. While you may hear *zoeken naar* (searching for), with general things like *werk* (work) or *hulp* (help), the preposition is usually dropped.
• **Uncountable Noun (*Werk*):** Just like in English, *werk* is an uncountable noun here, so it does not use an article like *een* (a). 

**Extensions:**
• Ik zoek een nieuwe baan. (I am looking for a new job.)
• Zoekt u een leuk cadeau? (Are you looking for a nice gift? - formal)
• Zij werkt in een grote supermarkt. (She works in a big supermarket.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Mijn broer zoekt werk in een druk restaurant. (My brother is looking for work in a busy restaurant.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, the informal *jij/je* is very common in daily life, even in many workplaces. However, when dealing with official institutions—such as the *gemeente* (municipality), the *UWV* (the government employment agency), or a formal recruitment agency—staff will initially address you with the polite *u*, making a sentence like this very common in official intake interviews.

u.form_note: 2nd person singular/plural formal subject pronoun. In A2 exam prompts, 'u' addresses you, the candidate. When answering, change 'u' to 'ik' (I).

zoekt.form_note: 2nd person formal (u) present tense of 'zoeken' (stem 'zoek' + -t). Placed in the second position (verb-second rule). When you reuse this verb with 'ik' in your exam answer, drop the -t: 'Ik zoek...'

werk.form_note: singular neuter noun (het-word), used here as an uncountable direct object without an article.
werk.fast_speech: often pronounced with a slight schwa between r and k: /ˈʋɛrək/

in.form_note: preposition of place, introducing the prepositional phrase 'in een winkel'.
in.fast_speech: links smoothly with the next word 'een': /ɪnən/

een.form_note: indefinite article used before singular countable nouns (both de- and het-words).
een.fast_speech: always pronounced with a short schwa /ən/, not like the number 'één' (/eːn/)

winkel.form_note: singular common gender noun (de-word), object of the preposition 'in'.

sentences.nl: In welke winkel werkt u liever?
sentences.en: In which shop would you rather work?
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **In** = In  
• **welke** = which  
• **winkel** = store / shop  
• **werkt** = work(s)  
• **u** = you (formal)  
• **liever?** = rather / preferably?  
*(Natural English: Which store do you prefer working in?)*

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Verb + *liever* (To prefer):** Dutch rarely uses a single verb for "to prefer." Instead, it combines the main action verb (here, *werken*) with the adverb *liever* (comparative of *graag*, meaning "rather" or "more gladly").  
• **Adjective Inflection (*welk* vs. *welke*):** Because *winkel* is a common gender noun (*de winkel*), the question word "which" takes an -e ending (*welke*). If it were a neuter noun (*het*-word) in the singular, it would be *welk* (e.g., *In welk huis...*).  
• **Inversion:** Because the sentence starts with a prepositional phrase (*In welke winkel*), the verb (*werkt*) comes immediately second, followed by the subject (*u*).  
• **Extensions:**  
  – *Welke koffie drinkt u liever?* (Which coffee do you prefer drinking?)  
  – *Op welke dag komt hij liever?* (On which day does he prefer to come?)  
  – *In welke stad woon je liever?* (In which city do you prefer living?)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Met welke collega eet u liever tijdens de pauze? (Which colleague do you prefer eating with during the break?)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• The pronoun **u** is the formal "you" in Dutch. While the Netherlands has become very informal and *je/jij* is standard in most workplaces, **u** is still used in job interviews, toward senior management in traditional sectors, or when speaking to older acquaintances and customers. Using *u* here suggests a polite, perhaps interview-like context.

in.form_note: starts the question phrase 'in welke winkel', which takes the first position in the sentence, forcing the verb 'werkt' into the second position

welke.form_note: inflected with -e because 'winkel' is a singular de-word ('welke' is used for all de-words and all plural nouns; 'welk' is only for singular het-words)

winkel.form_note: singular common-gender noun (de-word); object of the preposition 'in'

werkt.form_note: 2nd person formal (u) present tense of 'werken' (stem 'werk' + -t). Placed in the second position right after the question phrase 'In welke winkel' (inversion). In your answer, reuse this verb in the 'ik' form: 'Ik werk liever in...'
werkt.fast_speech: The final -t links smoothly to the vowel of 'u': /ʋɛrk.ty/

u.form_note: formal 2nd person subject pronoun; placed after the verb 'werkt' because of question inversion. In your answer, change 'u' to 'ik'

liever.form_note: irregular comparative of 'graag' (used with verbs to mean 'to like doing something'). 'Ik werk graag' = I like working; 'Ik werk liever' = I prefer working / would rather work

sentences.nl: Vertel ook waarom.
sentences.en: Also tell why.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **Vertel** = Tell  
• **ook** = also / too  
• **waarom** = why  

*(Natural translation: "Also tell [me] why.")*

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Imperative Mood (Gebiedende wijs):** The sentence starts with *Vertel*, which is the stem of the verb *vertellen* (to tell). In Dutch, to give an informal command, you simply use the verb stem at the very beginning of the sentence without a subject.  
• **Position of *ook*:** The adverb *ook* (also) comes immediately after the imperative verb to modify the entire command.  
• **Omitted Indirect Object:** Unlike English, where you usually need a pronoun after "tell" (e.g., "Tell *me* why"), Dutch frequently drops the pronoun in commands when it is obvious from the context.  
• **Extensions:**  
  – *Leg ook uit hoe.* (Also explain how.)  
  – *Vertel me alles.* (Tell me everything.)  
  – *Zeg maar waarom niet.* (Just say why not.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Kies je favoriete boek en vertel ook waarom. (Choose your favorite book and also tell [us] why.)  

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• **Dutch Directness & Debate Culture:** You will see this exact phrase constantly in Dutch school exams, job applications, and surveys. In Dutch culture, simply stating an opinion or a "yes/no" is rarely enough; you are almost always expected to substantiate (*onderbouwen*) your answer with arguments.

vertel.form_note: imperative (command form) of 'vertellen' (uses the verb stem; drop -en and reduce double 'll' to single 'l'). On the A2 speaking exam, 'Vertel...' prompts you to give more details.
vertel.fast_speech: The 'v' is often pronounced softly, almost like 'f': /fərˈtɛl/

ook.form_note: invariable adverb; placed right after the verb to add a second task to your exam answer.

waarom.form_note: interrogative adverb used here as a shortened indirect question after 'vertel'. On the exam, you answer this by starting a new main clause with 'Want...' (Because...) followed by subject + verb (verb-second word order).
waarom.fast_speech: The 'aa' is often shortened in casual speech: /ʋɑˈrɔm/

sentences.nl: Kies een van de plaatjes.
sentences.en: Choose one of the pictures.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **Kies** (Choose)  
• **een** (one)  
• **van** (of / from)  
• **de** (the)  
• **plaatjes.** (little pictures / images.)

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Imperative mood:** *Kies* is the imperative (command) form of the verb *kiezen* (to choose). In Dutch, commands are formed simply by using the verb stem (the *ik*-form) and placing it at the very beginning of the sentence.  
• **Diminutive plural:** *Plaatjes* is the plural diminutive of *de plaat* (plate/print/record). Adding *-je* makes a noun diminutive, and adding *-s* makes it plural. While literally meaning "little pictures," *plaatje* is the standard, everyday Dutch word for an illustration, graphic, or image in a book or on a screen.  
• **Partitive structure:** The phrase *een van de* + [plural noun] works just like the English "one of the...". Note that in writing, it is often written as *één* with accents to emphasize the number "one" rather than the indefinite article "a".

**Extensions:**  
• *Kies een van de opties.* (Choose one of the options.)  
• *Pak een van de koekjes.* (Take/grab one of the cookies.)  
• *Kijk naar de plaatjes in het boek.* (Look at the pictures in the book.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Kies een van de drie deuren om verder te gaan. (Choose one of the three doors to continue.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, "sparen voor plaatjes" (collecting pictures/stickers) is a massive cultural phenomenon, especially through supermarkets like Albert Heijn. Shoppers receive *plaatjes* (often of football players, local history, or nature) with their groceries to glue into collector's albums.

kies.form_note: imperative (command form) of 'kiezen' (uses the ik-form; z becomes s at the end of a word). In your exam answer, reuse this verb after 'Ik': 'Ik kies plaatje 1, want...'

een.form_note: functions here as the number 'one' (often written 'één' for clarity), not the article 'a/an', so it gets full vowel stress
een.fast_speech: unlike the article 'een' (/ən/), this is stressed and always pronounced with a long 'ee': /eːn/

van.form_note: used in the partitive construction 'een van de...' (one of the...)

de.form_note: plural definite article; all plural nouns in Dutch take 'de', even Diminutive het-words like 'het plaatje'

plaatjes.form_note: plural of 'plaatje' (which is the diminutive of 'de plaat'): all diminutives (-je) form their plural by adding -s

sentences.nl: Ik werk liever in de winkel met de lampen, want die winkel ziet er gezellig uit.
sentences.en: I would rather work in the shop with the lamps, because that shop looks cozy.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **Ik** (I) **werk** (work) **liever** (rather / preferably) **in de winkel** (in the shop) **met de lampen** (with the lamps), **want** (because / for) **die winkel** (that shop) **ziet** (sees/looks) **er** (there/it) **gezellig** (cozy) **uit** (out).  
• *Natural translation: I prefer working in the lamp shop, because that shop looks cozy.*

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Liever (Preference):** *Liever* is the comparative form of *graag* (gladly). While English uses a verb ("I prefer to work"), Dutch adds the adverb *liever* to the main verb (*Ik werk liever* = I work more-gladly).  
• **Coordinating Conjunction (want):** *Want* means "because." Unlike *omdat* (which pushes the verb to the end of the clause), *want* does not change the word order. The clause following *want* keeps normal Subject-Verb order (*die winkel ziet...*).  
• **Er ... uitzien (To look/appear):** This is a split pronominal verb meaning "to look [adjective]." In a main clause, it splits into three parts: the conjugated verb (*ziet*), the word *er*, and the separable prefix *uit* at the end. The adjective goes between *er* and *uit*.  

**Extensions:**  
• Ik drink **liever** thee, **want** koffie is te sterk. (I prefer drinking tea, because coffee is too strong.)  
• Dat huis **ziet er** heel oud **uit**. (That house looks very old.)  
• Hij blijft **liever** thuis, **want** het regent. (He prefers staying home, because it is raining.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Ik eet liever in het kleine café, want die plek ziet er heel rustig uit. (I prefer eating in the small café, because that place looks very quiet.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• **Gezellig:** This is arguably the most famous untranslatable Dutch word. While it translates here as "cozy" or "inviting," it encompasses everything from a warm atmosphere and good company to a pleasant, comforting vibe. Calling a shop, café, or living room *gezellig* is the ultimate Dutch compliment for an interior space.

sentences.nl: In een brillenwinkel.
sentences.en: In a glasses shop.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **In** = In  
• **een** = a  
• **brillenwinkel** = glasses-shop (brillen = glasses + winkel = shop)  

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Compound Nouns:** Dutch frequently combines two nouns into one word. Here, *bril* (singular: glasses) becomes plural *brillen*, and attaches to *winkel* (shop) to make *brillenwinkel*. In Dutch compounds, the plural form is often used as the first part to act as a glue (the *-en* sound) or because the shop sells multiple items.  
• **Articles and Gender:** The gender of a compound noun is always determined by the **last** word. Since it is *de winkel* (common gender), it is also *de brillenwinkel*. Here, the indefinite article *een* (a/an) is used, which is the same for all singular nouns regardless of gender.  
• **Extensions:**  
  • In een boekenwinkel. (In a bookstore.)  
  • In een schoenenwinkel. (In a shoe store.)  
  • Ik werk in een kledingwinkel. (I work in a clothing store.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Zij zoekt een nieuw montuur in een brillenwinkel. (She is looking for a new frame in an optician's shop.)  

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• While *brillenwinkel* is a very common and natural everyday word, the formal term you will often see on storefronts or hear in professional contexts is **opticien** (optician). For example, Dutch people frequently say, "Ik moet even naar de opticien" (I quickly need to go to the optician). In the Netherlands, eye tests (*oogmetingen*) at major *brillenwinkels* are usually free if you buy glasses there.

in.form_note: Introduces a short prepositional phrase answering a 'where' question (Waar...?). In the A2 speaking exam, you can make a fuller sentence by reusing the question's verb in second position, e.g., 'Ik ben in een brillenwinkel.'

een.form_note: Indefinite article used before singular countable nouns (both de- and het-words).

brillenwinkel.form_note: Singular de-word. Compound noun made from 'brillen' (plural of 'bril': double the consonant l to keep the short /ɪ/ vowel, add -en) + 'winkel' (shop).
brillenwinkel.fast_speech: The linking -n- in the middle is usually dropped in natural speech: /ˈbrɪləˌʋɪŋkəl/.

sentences.nl: Ik vind het fijn om mensen te helpen met het uitzoeken van een nieuwe bril.
sentences.en: I like to help people with choosing a new pair of glasses.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **Ik vind het fijn** – I find it nice / I like it  
• **om mensen te helpen** – to people to help (to help people)  
• **met het uitzoeken** – with the picking-out / choosing  
• **van een nieuwe bril.** – of a new glasses (of a new pair of glasses).  
*(Natural translation: I enjoy helping people choose a new pair of glasses.)*

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Ik vind het [adjective] om ... te [verb]:** This is a very common Dutch structure used to express an opinion about an action. "Het" acts as a placeholder for the action that follows. The action itself is framed inside the **om ... te + infinitive** construction, where the main verb goes to the end of that clause (*om mensen te helpen*).  
• **Het + infinitive + van (Nominalization):** In Dutch, you can turn a verb into a noun by placing the article *het* in front of the infinitive (*uitzoeken* = to pick out/choose → *het uitzoeken* = the choosing). To connect the object to this new noun, you must add the preposition **van** (of).  
• **Singular "bril":** While "glasses" is plural in English, *een bril* is always singular in Dutch.  
• **Extensions:**  
  – *Ik vind het leuk om boeken te lezen.* (I like reading books.)  
  – *Zij vindt het moeilijk om een cadeau uit te zoeken.* (She finds it difficult to pick out a gift.)  
  – *Kun je mij helpen met het maken van mijn huiswerk?* (Can you help me with doing my homework?)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Ik vind het leuk om mijn vrienden te helpen met het organiseren van een groot feest. (I enjoy helping my friends organize a big party.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch retail—especially at opticians (*de opticien*) or specialty shops—customer service tends to be very direct, honest, and consultative. If a pair of glasses doesn't suit your face, a Dutch shop assistant will likely tell you plainly (*"Deze staat u niet zo goed"*) and actively help you *uitzoeken* (select) a better pair, which is appreciated as genuine helpfulness rather than rudeness.

sentences.nl: Ik kies het tweede plaatje.
sentences.en: I choose the second picture.
sentences.note: Meester's reference answer, built from the topic bank.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Ik (I) / kies (choose) / het (the) / tweede (second) / plaatje (little-picture).

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Verb Conjugation:** *Kies* is the first-person singular (ik) form of the irregular verb *kiezen* (to choose). Notice the spelling and sound change: the *z* in the infinitive becomes an *s* at the end of the syllable.  
• **Diminutives and Gender:** *Plaatje* is the diminutive form of *de plaat* (plate/print/record), formed by adding the suffix *-je*. In Dutch, **all** diminutive singular nouns use the article *het*, regardless of the base word's original gender. While it literally means "little picture," *plaatje* is the standard everyday word for an image or illustration in a book, on a screen, or in a test.  
• **Ordinal Numbers:** *Tweede* (second) is created by adding *-de* to the cardinal number *twee* (two). Just like adjectives, ordinal numbers take an *-e* at the end when placed after a definite article (*de* or *het*).

**Extensions:**  
• Jij kiest de eerste optie. (You choose the first option.)  
• Wij bekijken het derde plaatje. (We look at the third picture.)  
• Welk plaatje kies je? (Which picture do you choose?)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Zij kiest altijd het mooiste liedje. (She always chooses the prettiest song.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• This exact sentence is a staple of the *Inburgeringsexamen* (Dutch civic integration exam) and language courses, where learners frequently have to describe or select images during speaking and listening tasks.  
• Additionally, *plaatje* is used idiomatically in Dutch to describe something that looks perfect: *"Het is een plaatje!"* (Literally: "It's a little picture!", meaning "It's a beauty!" or "It's picture-perfect!").

sentences.nl: Ik werk liever in de brillenwinkel, want ik help graag mensen.
sentences.en: I would rather work in the glasses shop, because I like helping people.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Ik (I) werk (work) liever (rather/preferably) in (in) de (the) brillenwinkel (glasses shop), want (because) ik (I) help (help) graag (gladly) mensen (people).

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Graag vs. Liever:** In Dutch, instead of saying "I like to [verb]", you use the verb + the adverb *graag* (gladly). *Liever* is the comparative form of *graag*, meaning "more gladly" or "rather/prefer to". 
• **Coordinating Conjunction (*want*):** *Want* means "because" or "for". Unlike *omdat* (which sends the verb to the end of the clause), *want* is a coordinating conjunction. It does not change the word order of the second clause: Subject (*ik*) + Verb (*help*) + Rest (*graag mensen*).
• **Compound Noun:** *Brillenwinkel* is a compound noun made of *brillen* (glasses) + *winkel* (shop). 

**Extensions:**
• Ik drink graag koffie, maar ik drink liever thee. (I like drinking coffee, but I prefer drinking tea.)
• Hij blijft thuis, want hij is ziek. (He stays home, because he is sick.)
• Zij koopt een nieuwe bril in de brillenwinkel. (She buys new glasses in the glasses shop.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Ik kook liever thuis, want ik eet graag gezond. (I prefer to cook at home, because I like eating healthy.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In everyday Dutch, a *brillenwinkel* is also very commonly referred to as an *opticien* (optician). You will hear both used interchangeably when people talk about going to buy glasses or contact lenses.

ik.form_note: 1st person singular subject pronoun; starts the new main clause after 'want'

sentences.nl: Kijk naar de plaatjes.
sentences.en: Look at the pictures.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Kijk (Look)  
• naar (at / towards)  
• de (the)  
• plaatjes (pictures / little plates).

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Imperative (Command Form):** *Kijk* is the stem of the verb *kijken* (to look). In Dutch, commands are formed by simply putting the verb stem at the very beginning of the sentence without a subject.  
• **Preposition Combination:** Just like English pairs "look" with "at," Dutch pairs *kijken* with the preposition *naar* (which usually means "to" or "towards").  
• **Diminutive Plural:** *Plaatjes* is the plural of *plaatje* (a small picture or illustration), which comes from *plaat* (plate/print). Even though singular diminutives always use the article *het* (*het plaatje*), all plural nouns in Dutch take the article *de* (*de plaatjes*).  

**Extensions:**  
• Kijk naar mij. (Look at me.)  
• Luister naar de leraar. (Listen to the teacher.)  
• Wij kijken naar een leuke film. (We are watching/looking at a nice movie.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Kijk naar de mooie bloemen in de tuin. (Look at the beautiful flowers in the garden.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• While *foto* is used for a photograph and *schilderij* for a painting, *plaatje* is the everyday Dutch word for an illustration in a book, a graphic in a textbook, or a collectible sticker (like the very popular supermarket promotional cards collected by Dutch children). There is also a common idiom: *Het is een plaatje!* (It's a picture! / It looks stunning!).

kijk.form_note: imperative (command form) of 'kijken', which uses the verb stem (same as the 'ik' present tense form). On the A2 speaking exam, instructions often start with this command. In your answer, you will describe what you see (e.g., 'Ik zie...').

naar.form_note: fixed preposition that goes with the verb 'kijken': 'kijken naar' means 'to look at'.
naar.fast_speech: often reduced to /nər/ in unstressed fast speech

de.form_note: plural definite article; all plural nouns in Dutch take 'de', even though the singular is 'het plaatje'.

plaatjes.form_note: plural of 'plaatje' (which is the diminutive of 'plaat'): all diminutive nouns ending in -je form their plural by adding -s.
plaatjes.fast_speech: the /tj/ cluster often sounds like /tʃ/ (like English 'ch' in 'chat'): /ˈplaːtʃəs/

sentences.nl: Wat drinkt u liever?
sentences.en: What would you rather drink?
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Wat = What  
• drinkt = drinks (do ... drink)  
• u = you (formal)  
• liever = rather / preferably  
• *Natural translation: What would you rather drink? / What do you prefer to drink?*

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Liever (Preference):** Instead of using a separate verb like "to prefer," Dutch uses the adverb *liever* (the comparative form of *graag*, meaning gladly/willingly) combined with a main verb.  
• **Question Word Order (Inversion):** Because the sentence starts with a question word (*Wat*), the conjugated verb (*drinkt*) comes immediately second, followed by the subject (*u*).  
• **Formal Pronoun:** *U* is the polite/formal form of "you." It takes the third-person singular verb form (stem + t: *drink* + *t*).  
• **Extensions:**  
– Wat eet je liever? (What would you rather eat? - *informal*)  
– Ik drink liever thee. (I prefer to drink tea / I'd rather drink tea.)  
– Waar woont u liever? (Where would you rather live? - *formal*)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Kijkt u vanavond liever een film of een serie? (Would you rather watch a movie or a series tonight?)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• When visiting a Dutch home or attending a business meeting, you will almost immediately be offered a drink—usually coffee (*koffie*) or tea (*thee*). Using *u* is standard in hospitality, shops, or when speaking to elders and strangers, though the Netherlands is quickly becoming more informal (shifting toward *je/jij*).

wat.meaning: what (the direct object of the sentence, asking about a thing/drink)
wat.form_note: interrogative pronoun placed in the first position to start an open question

drinkt.form_note: present tense of 'drinken' for 'u' (formal second-person singular): stem 'drink' + -t. Placed in second position right after the question word. To answer the question with 'ik', reuse this verb without the -t: 'Ik drink liever...'
drinkt.fast_speech: The final -t is often dropped before a vowel in casual speech, making 'drinkt u' sound like /drɪŋk y/

u.form_note: formal second-person singular subject pronoun; placed after the verb because of question inversion. Change this to 'ik' when answering the question.

liever.form_note: irregular comparative form of 'graag' (gladly/like to); used with a verb to ask about or express a preference between options

sentences.nl: Vertel ook wanneer u dit graag drinkt.
sentences.en: Also tell when you like to drink this.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Vertel (Tell) / ook (also) / wanneer (when) / u (you [formal]) / dit (this) / graag (gladly/like to) / drinkt (drink).  
• Natural translation: Also tell (us/me) when you like to drink this.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Imperative Mood:** *Vertel* is the stem of the verb *vertellen* (to tell) and is used at the very beginning of the sentence to give an instruction or command.  
• **Subordinate Clause Word Order:** The word *wanneer* (when) acts as a subordinating conjunction here. In Dutch, this kicks the conjugated verb of that clause (*drinkt*) all the way to the end of the sentence.  
• **Using "graag":** Instead of using a separate verb for "to like," Dutch often pairs a regular action verb with the adverb *graag* (gladly). Thus, *drinkt graag* translates naturally to "likes to drink."  

**Extensions:**  
• *Vertel ook waar u woont.* (Also tell where you live.)  
• *Ik eet dit graag in de zomer.* (I like to eat this in the summer.)  
• *Weet jij wanneer de film begint?* (Do you know when the movie starts?)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Laat ook weten waarom u dit boek graag leest. (Also let us know why you like to read this book.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• **The Formal "U" and Exam Prompts:** The pronoun *u* is the polite/formal version of "you," used with strangers, elders, or in professional contexts. Because this sentence combines an imperative instruction (*Vertel ook...*) with the formal *u*, it is classic "exam Dutch." You will see this exact phrasing constantly in prompts for the speaking and writing sections of the Dutch *Inburgeringsexamen* (civic integration exam) or *Staatsexamen NT2*, as well as in customer marketing surveys.

vertel.form_note: imperative (command form) of 'vertellen' (stem of the verb). On the A2 speaking exam, prompts starting with 'Vertel...' introduce an indirect question.
vertel.fast_speech: The prefix 'ver-' is unstressed and reduced to /vər/ or /və/.

ook.form_note: Adverb adding a second task to the exam prompt; placed right after the imperative verb.

wanneer.form_note: Introduces an indirect question after 'Vertel'. Because this is a subordinate clause (bijzin), it pushes the conjugated verb ('drinkt') to the very end of the sentence. When you answer, you can start with 'Ik drink dit graag wanneer...' or 'Ik drink dit graag in de ochtend.'
wanneer.fast_speech: Often pronounced with a short first vowel and weak stress: /ʋəˈneːr/.

u.form_note: 2nd person singular/plural formal subject pronoun. In your exam answer, you change 'u' to 'ik' (I).

dit.form_note: Demonstrative pronoun used for 'het'-words or to refer to a general thing mentioned earlier (like coffee, tea, or water). Direct object of 'drinkt'.

graag.form_note: Adverb used with a verb to mean 'like to [verb]' (u drinkt graag = you like to drink). Reuse this in your answer: 'Ik drink dit graag...' (with verb-second word order!).
word_forms: superlative: het liefst (most of all / prefer most)

drinkt.form_note: 2nd person formal ('u') present tense of 'drinken' (stem + t). Placed at the end of the sentence because it is in an indirect question after 'Vertel ... wanneer'. To answer the exam question, reuse this verb in the 1st person ('ik drink') in second position: 'Ik drink dit graag...' and add 'want...' + main clause.
drinkt.fast_speech: The /k/ between /ŋ/ and /t/ is often barely audible in natural speech: /drɪŋ(k)t/.

grammarHits.explanation: wanneer (when) starts the clause; drinkt goes to the end.

sentences.nl: Ik kies het eerste plaatje.
sentences.en: I choose the first picture.
sentences.note: Meester's reference answer, built from the topic bank.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **Ik** (I) **kies** (choose) **het** (the) **eerste** (first) **plaatje** (little picture / image).

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Diminutives (-je):** *Plaatje* is the diminutive of *de plaat* (plate/slab/record). Adding *-je* changes the meaning specifically to "picture" or "image". Crucially, all diminutive nouns in Dutch become neuter and take the article **het** in the singular, regardless of their original gender.  
• **Ordinal Numbers:** *Eerste* (first) acts like an adjective here. Because it is preceded by the definite article *het*, it takes the standard **-e** ending.  
• **Verb Conjugation:** *Kies* is the first-person singular present tense of the strong verb *kiezen* (to choose).  

**Extensions:**  
• Ik kies de laatste optie. (I choose the last option.)  
• Welk plaatje vind jij het mooist? (Which picture do you like the best?)  
• Hij leest het eerste hoofdstuk. (He reads the first chapter.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Zij kiest altijd het grootste koekje uit de trommel. (She always chooses the biggest cookie from the tin.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch, *plaatje* is the standard, everyday word for an illustration in a book, a sticker you collect at the supermarket, or a digital image on a computer. Additionally, the idiom *Het is een plaatje!* (Literally: "It is a little picture!") is very commonly used to mean "It's a beauty!" or "It looks picture-perfect!" (often said about a nice house, a cute baby, or a well-dressed person).

ik.form_note: first-person singular subject pronoun; starts the sentence so the verb comes second
ik.fast_speech: often reduced to /ək/ in unstressed positions, though usually clear at the start of a sentence

kies.form_note: first-person singular (ik) present tense of kiezen (z becomes s at the end of a syllable); placed in second position (verb-second rule) and reuses the exam question's verb (e.g., 'Welk plaatje kiest u?')

het.form_note: definite article for singular neuter (het) nouns; used here because 'plaatje' is a diminutive, and all diminutives are het-words
het.fast_speech: usually pronounced /ət/ in natural speech

eerste.form_note: ordinal number from 'een' (one); ordinal numbers always end in -e before a noun

plaatje.form_note: singular diminutive of 'de plaat' (plate/print/record), formed by adding -je; all diminutives take 'het' in the singular and mean 'picture' in this context

sentences.nl: Ik drink liever sinaasappelsap.
sentences.en: I would rather drink orange juice.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **Ik** = I  
• **drink** = drink  
• **liever** = rather / preferably  
• **sinaasappelsap** = orange juice (literally: *sinaasappel* [orange] + *sap* [juice])  
• *Natural translation: I would rather drink orange juice / I prefer drinking orange juice.*

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Expressing Preference with *Liever*:** In English, preference is often expressed with the verb "to prefer" or the phrase "would rather." In Dutch, you simply take the main action verb and add the adverb **liever** (the comparative form of *graag*, meaning "gladly/ willingly") right after the conjugated verb.  
• **Compound Nouns:** **Sinaasappelsap** is a compound noun made of *sinaasappel* (orange, literally "China-apple") and *sap* (juice). In Dutch, compound nouns are written together as a single word.  
• **Extensions:**  
  – Ik eet liever thuis. (I prefer eating at home / I'd rather eat at home.)  
  – Zij gaat liever met de trein. (She would rather go by train.)  
  – Drink je liever koffie of thee? (Do you prefer drinking coffee or tea?)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Ik lees liever een boek in het weekend. (I prefer reading a book on the weekend.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, when ordering at a café or restaurant, you will very often hear and see the French loanword **jus d'orange** (pronounced roughly as *zjuu-do-ranzj*) or simply **jus** instead of *sinaasappelsap*, especially when referring to freshly squeezed orange juice. *Sinaasappelsap* is more commonly used for juice from a carton in the supermarket.

ik.form_note: first-person singular subject pronoun; starts the main clause in position 1

drink.form_note: first-person singular (ik) present tense of drinken (stem only); placed in the verb-second (V2) position, reusing the verb from a speaking-exam question like 'Wat drink je?'

liever.form_note: irregular comparative of graag; placed directly after the finite verb 'drink' to express preference ('would rather drink')

sinaasappelsap.form_note: singular neuter compound noun (sinaasappel 'orange' + sap 'juice'); used here without an article as an uncountable direct object
sinaasappelsap.fast_speech: often shortened in casual speech to 'sinasappelsap' /ˈsinɑsˌɑpəlsɑp/ or 'jus d'orange'

sentences.nl: Ik drink het bij het ontbijt.
sentences.en: I drink it at breakfast.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Ik (I) drink (drink) het (it) bij (with / at) het (the) ontbijt (breakfast).  
• Natural translation: "I drink it with breakfast." / "I drink it at breakfast."

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Double meaning of "het":** The word *het* is used twice here with two different grammatical functions. The first *het* is an object pronoun meaning "it". The second *het* is the definite article ("the") for neuter nouns, as *ontbijt* is a *het*-word (*het ontbijt*).  
• **Preposition "bij":** When talking about food, drinks, or meals, the Dutch use the preposition *bij* to mean "with" or "accompanying" (as in, "having a drink *with* a meal"), rather than *met* (which would mean mixed together).  
• **Articles with meals:** Unlike English, which drops the article ("at breakfast"), Dutch almost always requires the definite article before meals (*bij het ontbijt*, *tijdens de lunch*).  

**Extensions:**  
• Wij eten brood bij de soep. (We eat bread with the soup.)  
• Drink jij melk bij de lunch? (Do you drink milk at lunch?)  
• Hij leest de krant bij het ontbijt. (He reads the newspaper at breakfast.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Zij drinkt altijd een kopje groene thee bij het ontbijt. (She always drinks a cup of green tea with breakfast.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• A traditional Dutch *ontbijt* is quick, simple, and rarely cooked. It typically consists of sliced bread (*boterhammen*) topped with cheese (*kaas*), cold cuts, or chocolate sprinkles (*hagelslag*). The standard drinks to have "bij het ontbijt" are strong coffee, tea, or a glass of cold milk (as the Dutch are huge dairy consumers).

ik.form_note: first-person singular subject pronoun; starts the main clause in position 1
ik.fast_speech: often reduced to /k/ and attached to the verb in rapid speech: /kdʀɪŋk/

drink.form_note: first-person singular (ik) present tense of the strong verb 'drinken'; sits in the verb-second (V2) position, reusing the main verb from the exam question (e.g., 'Wanneer drink je sap?')

het.form_note: definite article for singular neuter ('het') nouns; Dutch uses the article with meals after 'bij' ('bij het ontbijt' = 'at breakfast')
het.fast_speech: usually reduced to /ət/ ('t): 'bij 't ontbijt' /bɛi̯ ət ɔntˈbɛi̯t/

bij.form_note: preposition used with meals to mean 'at' or 'with' (literally 'by/near')

ontbijt.form_note: singular neuter noun (het-word), object of the preposition 'bij'
ontbijt.fast_speech: the /t/ before /b/ is often unreleased or assimilates slightly to /mpb/ or /nb/ in rapid speech

sentences.nl: U gaat op vakantie met de fiets.
sentences.en: You are going on holiday by bike.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• U (You - formal) gaat (go) op (on) vakantie (vacation) met (with/by) de (the) fiets (bicycle).  
• Natural translation: You are going on vacation by bicycle.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Formal Pronoun (*U*):** *U* is the polite/formal way to say "you" (singular or plural). Even though it means "you," it conjugates like a third-person singular verb (hij/zij/het), which is why the verb *gaan* (to go) becomes *gaat*.  
• **Fixed Preposition (*op vakantie*):** In Dutch, just like in English, the fixed preposition for vacation is *op* (on). The expression *op vakantie gaan* means "to go on vacation."  
• **Mode of Transport (*met de...*):** To express traveling "by" a certain vehicle in Dutch, you use the preposition *met* (with) followed by the definite article (*de* or *het*). Here, *fiets* is a *de*-word, so it is *met de fiets* (literally: with the bike).  
• **Extensions:**  
  – Wij gaan op vakantie met de auto. (We are going on vacation by car.)  
  – U gaat naar het werk met de trein. (You [formal] go to work by train.)  
  – Gaat u morgen met de bus? (Are you [formal] going by bus tomorrow?)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Mijn buren gaan dit jaar op vakantie met de trein. (My neighbors are going on vacation by train this year.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Cycling is deeply ingrained in Dutch culture, not just for daily commuting, but also for leisure. Going on a *fietsvakantie* (cycling holiday)—where people pack pannier bags and cycle from campsite to campsite or hotel to hotel across the Netherlands or Europe—is a very popular and traditional way for the Dutch to spend their summer holidays.

u.form_note: formal 2nd-person pronoun (singular or plural), subject of the sentence. In the A2 exam, when the prompt addresses you as 'u', change 'u' to 'ik' in your answer.

gaat.form_note: present tense, 2nd person formal (u) of 'gaan'. It sits in the second position (verb-second rule). When answering the exam question with 'Ik...', reuse this verb as 'Ik ga...'.

op.form_note: fixed preposition used with 'vakantie' ('op vakantie gaan' = to go on holiday).

vakantie.form_note: singular common-gender (de) noun; used without an article inside the fixed expression 'op vakantie'.

met.form_note: preposition used with 'de' + vehicle to express means of transport ('met de fiets' = by bike).

de.form_note: definite article for singular common-gender (de) nouns like 'fiets'; Dutch requires the article in transport phrases ('met de fiets').
de.fast_speech: after 'met', the /t/ and /d/ merge so 'met de' sounds like /ˈmɛdə/

fiets.form_note: singular common-gender (de) noun, object of the preposition 'met'.

sentences.nl: Waar fietst u liever?
sentences.en: Where would you rather cycle?
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **Waar** = Where  
• **fietst** = cycle / bike (conjugated for you/he/she)  
• **u** = you (formal)  
• **liever?** = rather / more gladly?  
• *Natural translation: Where do you prefer to cycle?*

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Verb + *liever* (To prefer):** In English, we use the verb "to prefer." In Dutch, it is much more common to use the main action verb combined with the adverb **liever** (the comparative form of *graag*, meaning "gladly/rather").  
• **Question Word Order (Inversion):** Because the sentence starts with a question word (*Waar*), the verb (*fietst*) must come second, immediately followed by the subject (*u*).  
• **Noun becomes Verb:** *Fiets* is a noun (bicycle), and *fietsen* is the verb (to cycle). With the formal pronoun *u*, the verb takes the stem + t (*fietst*).

**Extensions:**  
• Wat drinkt u liever, koffie of thee? (What do you prefer to drink, coffee or tea?)  
• Ik wandel liever in het bos. (I prefer walking in the forest / I rather walk in the forest.)  
• Waar woon je liever? (Where do you prefer to live? - *informal*)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Waar werkt u liever, thuis of op kantoor? (Where do you prefer to work, at home or at the office?)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Cycling is a massive part of Dutch daily life, not just for commuting, but also for recreation. It is very common to make small talk with older people or acquaintances (using the polite *u*) about their favorite recreational cycling routes—such as through the dunes (*in de duinen*), the forest (*in het bos*), or the countryside (*in de polder*).

waar.form_note: interrogative adverb asking about a place; starts the question so the verb comes second (inversion)

fietst.form_note: 2nd person formal (u) present tense of fietsen (stem fiets + -t); in your A2 answer, change this to 1st person singular: 'Ik fiets...'

u.form_note: 2nd person singular/plural formal subject pronoun; placed after the verb because of question word order (inversion)

liever.form_note: irregular comparative of graag (gladly); expresses preference ('would rather'); reuse it in your answer: 'Ik fiets liever in het park...'

sentences.nl: Vertel ook waarom.
sentences.en: Also tell why.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Vertel (Tell) | ook (also) | waarom (why).  
• Natural translation: Also tell me why. / Explain why, too.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Imperative Mood (Gebiedende wijs):** *Vertel* is the imperative (command) form of the verb *vertellen* (to tell/narrate). In Dutch, you form the informal imperative by simply using the verb stem (the *ik*-form) and dropping the subject pronoun.  
• **Verb-First Word Order:** Because this is a command, the verb (*Vertel*) comes at the very beginning of the sentence.  
• **Ellipsis (Implied Clause):** *Waarom* (why) normally introduces a subclause, which sends the verb to the end. Here, the rest of the clause is left unsaid because it is understood from context (e.g., *Vertel ook waarom [je dat denkt]* – Tell also why [you think that]).  

**Extensions:**  
• Leg ook uit hoe. (Also explain how.)  
• Vertel eens wat meer. (Tell [me] a bit more.)  
• Vraag ook wanneer hij komt. (Also ask when he is coming.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Kies je favoriete boek en vertel ook waarom. (Choose your favorite book and also tell why.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• This exact phrasing is ubiquitous in Dutch education and exams. Dutch school culture heavily emphasizes critical thinking and forming your own opinion. Simply answering "yes" or "no" is rarely enough; teachers and textbooks almost always add *"Vertel ook waarom"* or *"Leg uit waarom"* to prompt you to justify your answer.

vertel.form_note: imperative (command form) of 'vertellen': uses the stem (infinitive minus -en, double l becomes single l). In the A2 exam, this tells you to give extra information.
vertel.fast_speech: initial /v/ is often pronounced softly like /f/: /fərˈtɛl/

ook.form_note: adverb adding a second task to the exam prompt; placed right after the imperative verb

waarom.form_note: interrogative adverb used after 'vertel' to ask for a reason. In your A2 exam answer, you do not need a difficult indirect question; simply answer this part by starting a new main clause with 'Want...' (Because... + subject + verb).
waarom.fast_speech: in connected speech, the first syllable is often shortened: /ʋɑˈrɔm/

sentences.nl: Kies één van de plaatjes.
sentences.en: Choose one of the pictures.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Kies – Choose  
• één – one  
• van – of  
• de – the  
• plaatjes – little pictures / images  

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Imperative Mood (Command):** *Kies* is the imperative (stem) form of the verb *kiezen* (to choose). Placing it at the very beginning of the sentence without a subject turns it into a direct instruction or command.  
• **Accent Marks for Emphasis:** In Dutch, the word *een* means both "a/an" and "one". By adding accent marks (*één*), it explicitly stresses the number "one" rather than the indefinite article "a".  
• **Diminutive Plural:** *Plaatjes* is the plural diminutive of *plaat* (plate/print/picture). While *plaat* can mean a large print or a vinyl record, the diminutive *plaatje* is the standard everyday word for a small picture, illustration, or image in a book or on a screen.  
• **Extensions:**  
  – Kies één van de opties. (Choose one of the options.)  
  – Bekijk de mooie plaatjes in het boek. (Look at the pretty pictures in the book.)  
  – Neem één van de koekjes. (Take one of the cookies.)  

## 3. Create a New Example

sentences.nl: Ik fiets liever in de natuur.
sentences.en: I would rather cycle in nature.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Ik – I  
• fiets – cycle / bike  
• liever – rather / preferably  
• in – in  
• de – the  
• natuur – nature  

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Expressing Preference with *liever*:** In English, we often say "I prefer to [verb]," using a separate verb for "prefer." In Dutch, it is much more common and natural to use the adverb **liever** (the comparative form of *graag*) directly after the main conjugated verb. It translates to "rather" or "prefer to."  
• **Verb *fietsen*:** The noun *de fiets* (the bicycle) turns into the verb *fietsen* (to cycle). For the first-person singular (*ik*), you drop the *-en* ending, leaving the stem: *ik fiets*.  
• **Definite Article with *natuur*:** Unlike English, which uses "in nature" without an article, Dutch requires the definite article *de* here: *in de natuur*.  
• **Extensions:**  
– Ik drink liever thee. (I prefer to drink tea / I'd rather drink tea.)  
– Wij wandelen graag in de natuur. (We like to walk in nature.)  
– Hij blijft vandaag liever thuis. (He prefers to stay home today.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Zij leest liever een boek in het park. (She prefers to read a book in the park.)  

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• While cycling is the primary mode of daily commuter transport in Dutch cities, recreational cycling in nature (*in de natuur*) is a massive weekend pastime. The Netherlands has a unique, nationwide "junction network" (*knooppuntennetwerk*)—a system of numbered signs along scenic nature paths that allows you to easily plan and follow leisurely bike routes through forests, dunes, and polders without needing a map.

sentences.nl: Ik vind de omgeving mooi.
sentences.en: I think the surroundings are beautiful.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **Ik** (I) **vind** (find / consider) **de** (the) **omgeving** (surroundings / area) **mooi** (beautiful).  
• *Natural translation:* I think the surroundings are beautiful.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Expressing Opinions with *Vinden*:** In Dutch, the verb *vinden* (literally "to find") is the standard way to express an opinion, equivalent to "I think [something] is [adjective]" in English. The structure is: Subject + *vinden* + Object + Adjective.  
• **Uninflected Adjective:** Because the adjective *mooi* comes after the noun it describes (acting as a predicate complement rather than sitting directly in front of the noun), it does not take an *-e* ending, even though *omgeving* is a *de*-word.  
• **Extensions:**  
  – *Ik vind deze film erg spannend.* (I think this movie is very exciting.)  
  – *Zij vindt het nieuwe huis een beetje te klein.* (She finds the new house a bit too small.)  
  – *Wat vind je van de omgeving?* (What do you think of the area/surroundings?)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Wij vinden de sfeer in dit restaurant heel gezellig. (We think the atmosphere in this restaurant is very cozy.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Using *Ik vind...* is the most common, direct way Dutch people share personal tastes and subjective opinions. Because the Netherlands is densely populated and largely flat, the word *omgeving* is frequently used when discussing the quality of a neighborhood, or when going on weekend walks or bike rides to appreciate local nature (e.g., *een bosrijke omgeving* – a wooded area).

sentences.nl: In de stad, want daar kun je makkelijk fietsen op fietspaden.
sentences.en: In the city, because you can easily cycle on bike paths there.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **In de stad** = In the city  
• **want** = because / for  
• **daar** = there  
• **kun je** = can you  
• **makkelijk** = easily  
• **fietsen** = cycle / bike (verb)  
• **op fietspaden** = on bike paths  

*(Natural translation: "In the city, because you can easily cycle on bike paths there.")*

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Coordinating Conjunction (*want*):** *Want* ("because") connects two main clauses and does **not** send the verb to the end of the sentence (unlike *omdat*).  
• **Inversion (*daar kun je*):** Even though *want* doesn't change the word order by itself, the clause after it starts with the location word *daar* ("there"). In Dutch, when a clause starts with a time or place word instead of the subject, the verb and subject swap places (*daar kun je* instead of *daar je kunt*). Note also that *kunt* drops the "-t" when *je* comes right after it (*kun je*).  
• **Generic "je":** Here, *je* ("you") is used in a general sense to mean "one" or "people in general."  
• **Compound Noun (*fietspaden*):** Formed from *fiets* (bike) + *paden* (paths). 

**Extensions:**  
• Ik blijf thuis, **want daar kun je** rustig werken. (I am staying home, because you can work quietly there.)  
• In het park, **want daar kun je makkelijk** wandelen op wandelpaden. (In the park, because you can easily walk on walking paths there.)  
• **Kun je makkelijk** parkeren in het centrum? (Can you easily park in the city center?)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Ik woon graag in Nederland, want daar kun je overal veilig op fietspaden rijden. (I like living in the Netherlands, because you can safely ride on bike paths everywhere there.)  

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• The Netherlands is world-famous for its cycling infrastructure, boasting over 35,000 kilometers of dedicated *fietspaden* (bike paths). These paths are usually paved in distinct red asphalt. As a pedestrian, be very careful not to accidentally walk on them—Dutch cyclists commute at high speeds and will quickly ring their bells (or shout) if you are blocking the lane!

sentences.nl: Ik kies het eerste plaatje.
sentences.en: I choose the first picture.
sentences.note: Meester's reference answer, built from the topic bank.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Ik – I  
• kies – choose  
• het – the  
• eerste – first  
• plaatje – picture (diminutive)  
• *Full natural translation: I choose the first picture.*

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Verb Conjugation:** *Kies* is the first-person singular (ik-form) present tense of the strong verb *kiezen* (to choose). Notice that the 'z' changes to an 's' at the end of the syllable, and the vowel is written with 'ie' to keep the sound long.  
• **Diminutives and Gender:** *Plaatje* is the diminutive form of *de plaat* (plate/print/record). In Dutch, **all** diminutive nouns (ending in *-je*, *-tje*, *-pje*, etc.) become neuter and take the definite article **het**, regardless of the original noun's gender.  
• **Ordinal Numbers:** *Eerste* (first) is an ordinal number. Like adjectives, ordinal numbers always end in **-e** when placed after *de* or *het*.  

• **Extensions:**  
  – *Zij kiest het tweede boekje.* (She chooses the second booklet.)  
  – *Welk plaatje kies jij?* (Which picture do you choose?)  
  – *Dit is mijn eerste keus.* (This is my first choice.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Hij bekijkt het laatste filmpje op zijn telefoon. (He watches the last short video on his phone.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• **The Power of the Diminutive:** Dutch speakers use diminutives (*verkleinwoorden*) constantly, not just to indicate physical smallness, but also to change the meaning of a word or make it sound friendlier. While *een foto* is specifically a photograph, *een plaatje* usually refers to an illustration, a digital image, a drawing in a children's book, or a collectible trading card (which are very popular in Dutch supermarket promotions). Calling someone or something *een plaatje* is also an idiom meaning "a beauty" (e.g., *De bruid was een plaatje* – The bride was a vision/picture-perfect).

• **Verb "fietsen":** In Dutch, modes of transport are often turned directly into verbs. *De fiets* (the bicycle) becomes *fietsen* (to cycle/to go by bike). *Ik fiets* is the first-person singular (stem of the verb).

sentences.nl: want het is daar rustig en mooi.
sentences.en: because it is quiet and beautiful there.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **want** – because / for  
• **het** – it  
• **is** – is  
• **daar** – there  
• **rustig** – quiet / peaceful  
• **en** – and  
• **mooi** – beautiful / nice  

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Coordinating Conjunction (*want*):** In Dutch, both *want* and *omdat* mean "because." However, *want* is a coordinating conjunction, which means it connects two main clauses and **does not** change the normal word order (Subject + Verb: *het is*). If you used *omdat*, the verb would be pushed to the very end of the sentence (*omdat het daar rustig en mooi **is***).  
• **Position of *daar*:** Place adverbs like *daar* (there) or *hier* (here) usually come right after the conjugated verb (*is*) and before the predicate adjectives (*rustig en mooi*).  
• **Predicate Adjectives:** Because *rustig* and *mooi* come after the verb *is* and do not sit directly in front of a noun, they remain in their base form and do not take an *-e* ending.  

**Extensions:**  
• Ik blijf binnen, **want het is** buiten koud. (I am staying inside, because it is cold outside.)  
• We gaan naar dat café, **want het is daar** erg gezellig. (We are going to that café, because it is very cozy there.)  
• Zij leest graag in de tuin, **want het is** hier **rustig**. (She likes reading in the garden, because it is quiet here.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Ik wandel graag in het bos, want het is daar fris en groen. (I like walking in the forest, because it is fresh and green there.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• The Netherlands is one of the most densely populated countries in Europe. Because cities in the *Randstad* (the central urban ring including Amsterdam, Rotterdam, The Hague, and Utrecht) are quite busy and compact, Dutch people highly value places that are *rustig* (quiet/calm) and *mooi* (scenic) for their weekend getaways, such as the Wadden Islands or the Veluwe national park.

sentences.nl: Deze spullen hangen in een leslokaal.
sentences.en: These things are hanging in a classroom.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Deze (These) spullen (stuff/things) hangen (hang/are hanging) in (in) een (a) leslokaal (classroom).  
• Natural English: "These things are hanging in a classroom."

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Posture Verbs for Location:** Instead of the generic verb *zijn* (to be), Dutch strongly prefers using "posture verbs" like *hangen* (to hang), *liggen* (to lie), and *staan* (to stand) to describe where an object is located.  
• **Plural Noun "Spullen":** *Spullen* translates to the uncountable English word "stuff" or the plural "things/belongings." Because it is grammatically plural in Dutch, it takes the demonstrative pronoun *deze* (these) and the plural verb *hangen*.  
• **Compound Noun:** *Leslokaal* is a compound of *les* (lesson) + *lokaal* (room/hall). Because *het lokaal* is a *het*-word, *het leslokaal* is also a *het*-word, though with the indefinite article *een* (a), the gender doesn't change the article.  

**Extensions:**  
• Mijn jassen hangen in de gang. (My coats are hanging in the hallway.)  
• Waar liggen mijn spullen? (Where is my stuff lying? / Where is my stuff?)  
• De studenten zitten in het leslokaal. (The students are sitting in the classroom.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Deze mooie schilderijen hangen in een groot museum. (These beautiful paintings are hanging in a big museum.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch schools, you will hear both *leslokaal* and *klaslokaal* for "classroom." *Klaslokaal* is slightly more common in primary and secondary education, whereas *leslokaal* or simply *lokaal* is very common in higher education, adult education, or for specific subject rooms (like a *muzieklokaal*).

sentences.nl: Vertel welke spullen dat zijn.
sentences.en: Tell which things those are.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Vertel (Tell) | welke (which) | spullen (stuff/things) | dat (that/those) | zijn (are).  
• Natural translation: "Tell [me] what kind of stuff that is" or "Tell [me] which things those are."

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Imperative (Gebiedende wijs):** *Vertel* is the command form of the verb *vertellen* (to tell). It is formed simply by using the verb stem, with no subject pronoun.  
• **Embedded Question & Word Order:** *Welke spullen dat zijn* is a subordinate clause (an indirect question). Because of this, the conjugated verb (*zijn*) is kicked to the very end of the sentence.  
• **Welk vs. Welke:** *Welke* is used here because *spullen* is plural. (You only use *welk* for singular *het*-words).  
• **Dat + zijn:** In Dutch, the singular neuter demonstrative pronoun *dat* (that) is used to point out plural nouns when followed by the linking verb *zijn* (are). So, "those are" translates to *dat zijn*.  
• **Spullen:** This is a plural-only noun in this context, meaning "stuff," "belongings," or "gear."

**Extensions:**  
• *Laat zien welke boeken dat zijn.* (Show [me] which books those are.)  
• *Ik weet niet welke spullen je bedoelt.* (I don't know which stuff you mean.)  
• *Zeg maar welke schoenen van jou zijn.* (Just say which shoes are yours.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Leg uit welke regels dat zijn. (Explain which rules those are.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Direct imperatives like *Vertel...* are grammatically fine, especially in instructions or rapid conversation. However, in everyday spoken Dutch, a bare command can sometimes feel a bit blunt or interrogation-like. Dutch speakers will almost always soften commands using modal particles like **eens** or **even**: *"Vertel eens welke spullen dat zijn"* (Tell me what kind of stuff that is).

vertel.form_note: imperative (command form) singular of 'vertellen' (inseparable verb with prefix ver-). In exam prompts, 'Vertel...' introduces an indirect question, which sends the verb of the next clause ('zijn') to the very end.

welke.form_note: interrogative determiner with -e ending because it modifies the plural noun 'spullen'. Here it introduces the indirect question after 'Vertel'.

spullen.form_note: plural noun (almost always used in the plural when meaning 'stuff/things'; singular 'het spul' exists and means 'material/stuff': double the consonant l to keep the short /ʏ/ vowel, add -en)

dat.form_note: demonstrative pronoun used as the subject of the clause. In Dutch, singular 'dat' (or 'dit') is used as the subject with the plural verb 'zijn' to point to plural things ('Dat zijn mijn spullen' = 'Those are my things'). When answering, start your main clause with 'Dat zijn...'.

It sits at the end of the sentence because 'welke spullen dat zijn' is an indirect question after 'Vertel'. To answer this exam question, reuse this verb in second position: 'Dat zijn...'

sentences.nl: Vertel ook wat de cursisten met de spullen kunnen doen.
sentences.en: Also tell what the students can do with the things.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Vertel (Tell) 
• ook (also) 
• wat (what) 
• de cursisten (the course participants / students) 
• met (with) 
• de spullen (the stuff / things) 
• kunnen (can) 
• doen (do).

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Imperative (Gebiedende wijs):** The sentence starts with the verb stem *Vertel* (from *vertellen*), which gives a direct command or instruction ("Tell...").
• **Indirect Question / Subordinate Clause:** The word *wat* introduces an indirect question. In Dutch subordinate clauses, all verbs are pushed to the very end of the sentence, creating the verb cluster *kunnen doen* (can do).
• **Vocabulary Note:** *Spullen* is a very common plural-only noun in everyday Dutch that translates to "stuff," "things," or "gear/supplies." *Cursisten* specifically refers to people taking a course (like a language or hobby course), rather than university students (*studenten*) or high school pupils (*leerlingen*).

• Extensions:
– *Laat ook zien wat de kinderen met de verf kunnen maken.* (Also show what the children can make with the paint.)
– *Ik weet niet wat ik met deze oude spullen moet doen.* (I don't know what I should do with this old stuff.)
– *Vraag even wat de cursisten van de les vinden.* (Just ask what the course participants think of the lesson.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Leg eerst uit wat de nieuwe collega's met deze documenten moeten doen. (First explain what the new colleagues have to do with these documents.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• As an adult learning Dutch, you will almost always be referred to as a *cursist* (or *taalcursist*). The Dutch education system strictly separates *leerlingen* (primary/secondary school), *studenten* (higher education/university), and *cursisten* (anyone taking a *cursus*—from integration classes and language courses to first-aid training).

sentences.nl: Gebruik alle plaatjes.
sentences.en: Use all the pictures.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Gebruik = Use  
• alle = all  
• plaatjes = (small) pictures / images  

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Imperative Mood (De gebiedende wijs):** "Gebruik" is the stem of the verb *gebruiken* (to use). Placed at the very beginning of the sentence without a subject, it forms a direct command or instruction.  
• **Diminutive Plural:** "Plaatjes" is the plural of *het plaatje* (small picture/illustration), which is the diminutive form of *de plaat* (plate/large print). Even though *plaatje* is a diminutive, it is the standard everyday word for an illustration, sticker, or digital image.  
• **Quantifier Agreement:** The word *al* (all) gets an *-e* ending and becomes *alle* when placed directly before a plural noun (like *plaatjes*) or a *de*-word.  

**Extensions:**  
• *Bekijk alle foto's.* (Look at all the photos.)  
• *Gebruik je fantasie.* (Use your imagination.)  
• *Verzamel alle voetbalplaatjes.* (Collect all the soccer cards/stickers.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Lees alle zinnen hardop voor. (Read all the sentences out loud.)  

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, collecting *plaatjes* (stickers or trading cards depicting sports players, animals, or historical figures) is a massive cultural phenomenon tied to supermarket promotions. Shoppers receive packs of *plaatjes* with their groceries to glue into collector albums, and it is very common to see children (and adults) trading them outside supermarkets like Albert Heijn or Jumbo.
