sentences.nl: Een schoolbord, een landkaart en een klok.
sentences.en: A blackboard, a map, and a clock.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Een (A) schoolbord (blackboard), een (a) landkaart (map) en (and) een (a) klok (clock).

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Indefinite Article:** The word *een* means "a" or "an." Unlike the definite articles (*de* and *het*), *een* is the same for all singular nouns regardless of gender. (For example: *het schoolbord*, *de landkaart*, *de klok* all just use *een*).  
• **Compound Nouns:** Dutch frequently glues words together to make new ones. *Schoolbord* = *school* (school) + *bord* (board). *Landkaart* = *land* (country/land) + *kaart* (map/card).  
• **Punctuation (No Oxford Comma):** In a list of items, Dutch does not use a comma before the word *en* (and).  

• **Extensions:**  
– Een tafel, een stoel en een kast. (A table, a chair, and a cupboard.)  
– Ik zie een grote landkaart. (I see a big map.)  
– De docent schrijft op het schoolbord. (The teacher writes on the blackboard.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• In het klaslokaal hangen een schoolbord, een landkaart en een klok aan de muur. (In the classroom, a blackboard, a map, and a clock are hanging on the wall.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• While *schoolbord* traditionally refers to a green or black chalkboard, almost all modern Dutch classrooms now use a *digibord* (an interactive digital whiteboard/smartboard). However, the word *schoolbord* is still widely understood and used in general contexts.

sentences.nl: Cursisten kunnen woorden op het schoolbord schrijven, de landen op de kaart aanwijzen en de tijd op de klok zien.
sentences.en: Students can write words on the blackboard, point out the countries on the map, and see the time on the clock.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Cursisten (Course participants / Adult students)  
• kunnen (can / are able to)  
• woorden (words)  
• op het schoolbord (on the blackboard)  
• schrijven, (to write,)  
• de landen (the countries)  
• op de kaart (on the map)  
• aanwijzen (to point out)  
• en (and)  
• de tijd (the time)  
• op de klok (on the clock)  
• zien. (to see.)  

*Natural translation: Course participants can write words on the blackboard, point out the countries on the map, and see the time on the clock.*

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Modal Verb + Infinitive at the End:** This sentence uses the modal verb *kunnen* (can) in the second position. In Dutch, all the main action verbs coupled with this modal verb (*schrijven*, *aanwijzen*, *zien*) must be pushed to the very end of their respective clauses in their infinitive form.  
• **Separable Verb (*aanwijzen*):** The verb *aanwijzen* (to point out / indicate) is separable (*aan* + *wijzen*). However, because it is used here as an infinitive at the end of the clause (thanks to *kunnen*), it stays glued together as one word.  
• **Preposition *op*:** In Dutch, *op* (on) is the standard preposition for surfaces where information is displayed, even if they are vertical in English (e.g., *op het bord*, *op de kaart*, *op de klok*).  

**Extensions:**  
• Jij kunt de fouten in de tekst aanwijzen. (You can point out the mistakes in the text.)  
• Ik kan niet op het schoolbord schrijven. (I cannot write on the blackboard.)  
• Wij kunnen de route op de kaart zien. (We can see the route on the map.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• De leraar kan de nieuwe zinnen op het scherm laten zien en de moeilijke woorden uitleggen. (The teacher can show the new sentences on the screen and explain the difficult words.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• **Cursisten vs. Studenten:** The word *cursist* (plural: *cursisten*) specifically refers to someone taking a *cursus* (a training course, workshop, or language class), usually in adult education. You will hear this word constantly in Dutch integration courses (*inburgeringscursus*) or evening language classes. By contrast, *leerlingen* is used for primary/high school pupils, and *studenten* is generally reserved for college or university students.

sentences.nl: In het lokaal hangt een soort computer om naar filmpjes te kijken, een plaat van de wereld om de landen te noemen en een klok om te zeggen hoe laat het is.
sentences.en: In the classroom hangs a kind of computer to watch videos on, a picture of the world to name the countries, and a clock to say what time it is.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• In het lokaal = In the classroom  
• hangt = hangs  
• een soort computer = a sort of computer  
• om naar filmpjes te kijken, = in order to at little-videos to look,  
• een plaat van de wereld = a poster/picture of the world  
• om de landen te noemen = in order the countries to name  
• en een klok = and a clock  
• om te zeggen = in order to say/tell  
• hoe laat het is. = how late it is (what time it is).  

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Inversion (Verb-Subject order):** Because the sentence starts with a location (*In het lokaal*), the verb (*hangt*) must come immediately second, before the subject (*een soort computer*).  
• **Posture Verb (*hangen*):** Dutch rarely uses the generic verb *zijn* (to be) to describe where objects are. Instead, it specifies posture: things either *liggen* (lie), *staan* (stand), or *hangen* (hang).  
• **Purpose Clause (*om ... te + infinitive*):** Used three times in this sentence, the structure *om* + [object/preposition] + *te* + [infinitive verb] means "in order to [do something]".  
• **Indirect Question Word Order:** At the very end (*hoe laat het is*), the verb *is* goes to the end because it is a subclause triggered by *hoe laat* (what time).  

**Extensions:**  
• *Op de muur hangt een groot bord om op te schrijven.* (On the wall hangs a big board to write on.)  
• *Ik gebruik mijn telefoon om naar muziek te luisteren.* (I use my phone to listen to music.)  
• *Kun je me zeggen hoe laat de les begint?* (Can you tell me what time the lesson begins?)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• In de keuken staat een grote tafel om aan te eten en hangt een kalender om de verjaardagen niet te vergeten. (In the kitchen stands a big table to eat at, and hangs a calendar so as not to forget the birthdays.)  

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• **Het digibord:** The phrase "een soort computer om naar filmpjes te kijken" hanging in a classroom almost certainly refers to a *digibord* (smartboard/interactive whiteboard), which has completely replaced traditional chalkboards in nearly all Dutch schools.  
• **Verjaardagskalender:** Notice how the Dutch use *hangen* for wall items. A classic cultural equivalent in the home is the *verjaardagskalender* (birthday calendar), which traditionally hangs in the *wc* (toilet room) so guests can see whose birthday is coming up.

sentences.nl: Ik zie een schoolbord, een landkaart en een klok.
sentences.en: I see a blackboard, a map and a clock.
sentences.note: Meester's reference answer, built from the topic bank.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Ik (I) zie (see) een (a) schoolbord (blackboard), een (a) landkaart (map) en (and) een (a) klok (clock).

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Basic Word Order (SVO):** The sentence uses the standard Subject-Verb-Object order: *Ik* (Subject) + *zie* (Verb, present tense of *zien*) + the list of items (Direct Objects).  
• **Indefinite Articles:** In Dutch, both *de*-words (common gender) and *het*-words (neuter gender) use the same indefinite article in the singular: **een** (a/an). Even though it is *het schoolbord*, *de landkaart*, and *de klok*, they all simply take *een* here.  
• **Compound Nouns:** Dutch merges nouns together to create single concepts: *school* (school) + *bord* (board) = *schoolbord*, and *land* (country/land) + *kaart* (map/card) = *landkaart*.

**Extensions:**  
• Ik zie een tafel, een stoel en een lamp. (I see a table, a chair, and a lamp.)  
• Wij zoeken een landkaart van Nederland. (We are looking for a map of the Netherlands.)  
• De leraar schrijft op het schoolbord. (The teacher writes on the blackboard.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• In het klaslokaal zie ik een bureau, een computer en een grote landkaart. (In the classroom, I see a desk, a computer, and a large map.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In modern Dutch schools, the traditional *schoolbord* (chalkboard) has almost entirely been replaced by the **digibord** (interactive smartboard), though the word *schoolbord* is still widely understood and used in learning materials.

sentences.nl: Je kunt op het schoolbord schrijven.
sentences.en: You can write on the blackboard.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Je (You) kunt (can) op (on) het (the) schoolbord (blackboard) schrijven (write / to write).  
• Natural translation: You can write on the blackboard.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Modal Verb Structure:** This sentence uses the modal verb *kunnen* (can/to be able to). In a Dutch main clause, the conjugated modal verb (*kunt*) takes the second position, and the main action verb goes to the very end of the sentence in its infinitive form (*schrijven*).  
• **Kunt vs. Kan:** With the pronoun *je* (you), both *je kunt* and *je kan* are grammatically correct. *Je kunt* is considered slightly more standard or formal, while *je kan* is very common in everyday spoken Dutch.  
• **Compound Noun:** *Schoolbord* is a neuter (*het*) compound noun made of *school* (school) + *bord* (board).  
• **Extensions:**  
  – *Je kunt in het schrift schrijven.* (You can write in the notebook.)  
  – *Hij kan op de muur tekenen.* (He can draw on the wall.)  
  – *Wij kunnen op het papier schrijven.* (We can write on the paper.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• De leraar kan met een krijtje op het schoolbord schrijven. (The teacher can write on the blackboard with a piece of chalk.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In modern Dutch schools, the traditional green or black *schoolbord* has been almost entirely replaced by the *digibord* (smartboard / interactive whiteboard). However, the word *schoolbord* (or simply *het bord*) is still widely understood and sometimes used generically by older generations to refer to the board at the front of the class.

sentences.nl: Je kunt op de kaart de landen zien.
sentences.en: You can see the countries on the map.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **Je** – You (can also mean "one" or "people" in general)  
• **kunt** – can  
• **op de kaart** – on the map  
• **de landen** – the countries  
• **zien.** – see.  
*(Natural English: You can see the countries on the map.)*

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Modal Verbs & Sentence Bracket:** *Kunt* is the second-person singular form of *kunnen* (can/to be able to). When using a modal verb, the conjugated modal verb takes the second position, and the main verb (*zien*) is pushed to the very end of the sentence in its infinitive form.  
• **Kan vs. Kunt:** With the pronoun *je/jij*, both *je kunt* and *je kan* are grammatically correct. *Je kunt* is slightly more formal and standard in written Dutch, while *je kan* is very common in spoken Dutch.  
• **Word Order in the Middle:** Notice that the prepositional phrase (*op de kaart*) comes before the direct object (*de landen*). In Dutch, place/location elements often precede the object, or they can be swapped depending on what you want to emphasize (*Je kunt de landen op de kaart zien* is also correct).  
• **False Friend Alert:** *De kaart* means "the map" here, though in other contexts it can mean "ticket," "menu," or "card" (like a postcard or playing card).

**Extensions:**  
• *Je kunt in het boek de antwoorden vinden.* (You can find the answers in the book.)  
• *We kunnen op het scherm de tijd zien.* (We can see the time on the screen.)  
• *Kun je op de foto mijn huis zien?* (Can you see my house in the photo?)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• *Je kunt op de menukaart alle gerechten lezen.* (You can read all the dishes on the menu.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch, the pronoun **je** (unstressed "you") is extremely common as an equivalent to the English "one" or general "you." Instead of using a passive structure like "The countries can be seen on the map," Dutch speakers strongly prefer active sentences using *je*, as in "You [anyone] can see the countries on the map."

sentences.nl: En je kunt op de klok de tijd zien.
sentences.en: And you can see the time on the clock.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• En (And)  
• je kunt (you can)  
• op de klok (on the clock)  
• de tijd (the time)  
• zien (see / to see).  
*Natural English: "And you can see the time on the clock."*

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Modal Verb and Word Order:** The verb *kunt* (from *kunnen*, "can") is a modal verb. In Dutch main clauses, the conjugated modal verb sits in the second position, and it pushes the main action verb in its infinitive form (*zien*) to the very end of the sentence.  
• **Kunt vs. Kan:** With the pronoun *je* (you), both *je kunt* and *je kan* are grammatically correct. *Je kunt* is considered slightly more standard or neat in written Dutch, while *je kan* is very common in spoken Dutch.  
• **Preposition Use:** Dutch uses the preposition *op* (on) for looking at instruments, screens, or surfaces to get information (e.g., *op de klok*, *op je telefoon*, *op de kaart*).  

**Extensions:**  
• Je kunt op het scherm de informatie lezen. (You can read the information on the screen.)  
• Ik kan op mijn horloge de tijd niet zien. (I cannot see the time on my watch.)  
• We kunnen op het bord de prijzen zien. (We can see the prices on the board.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• En je kunt op de kaart de juiste route zien. (And you can see the correct route on the map.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• When reading the clock in daily life, the Dutch use a "half-hour" system that looks forward to the next hour, unlike the English system which looks back. For example, 7:30 is called *half acht* (literally "half eight," meaning halfway to eight). Additionally, 7:20 is expressed relative to the half-hour: *tien voor half acht* (ten before half-eight). Being on time (*op tijd zijn*) is highly valued in Dutch culture!

sentences.nl: Ricardo werkt als kapper.
sentences.en: Ricardo works as a hairdresser.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Ricardo = Ricardo  
• werkt = works  
• als = as  
• kapper = hairdresser / barber  

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Omitting the article with professions:** Unlike in English ("works as *a* hairdresser"), Dutch omits the indefinite article (*een*) after the words *als* (as) or *zijn* (to be) when stating someone's profession, nationality, or function.  
• **Verb conjugation:** *Werkt* is the third-person singular (hij/zij/het) present tense form of the verb *werken* (to work). The stem is *werk* + *t*.  
• **Extensions:**  
  – Zij werkt als arts in het ziekenhuis. (She works as a doctor in the hospital.)  
  – Mijn broer is leraar. (My brother is a teacher.)  
  – Ik werk als vrijwilliger. (I work as a volunteer.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Sanne werkt als bakker in een klein dorp. (Sanne works as a baker in a small village.)  

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch, it is increasingly common to use the grammatically masculine form of a profession (like *kapper* or *leraar*) as a gender-neutral term for everyone, though specific feminine forms (*kapster*, *lerares*) still exist and are used.

sentences.nl: Kijk naar de plaatjes.
sentences.en: Look at the pictures.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Kijk (Look)  
• naar (at / towards)  
• de (the)  
• plaatjes (pictures / little plates).  

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Imperative Mood:** *Kijk* is the command form of the verb *kijken* (to look). In Dutch, the singular imperative is simply the verb stem, with the subject pronoun (*jij/je*) dropped.  
• **Fixed Preposition:** The verb *kijken* always pairs with the preposition *naar* to mean "to look at."  
• **Diminutive Plural:** *Plaatjes* is the plural of *plaatje* (picture/image). It comes from *plaat* (plate/panel) + the diminutive suffix *-je* + the plural *-s*. Even though singular diminutives use the article *het* (*het plaatje*), all plural nouns in Dutch use the article *de* (*de plaatjes*).  

**Extensions:**  
• Kijk naar mij. (Look at me.)  
• Luister naar de muziek. (Listen to the music.)  
• Wij kijken naar een leuke film. (We are watching a nice movie.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Kijk naar de mooie bloemen in de tuin. (Look at the beautiful flowers in the garden.)  

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• While *plaatje* literally means a small plate, it is the standard everyday word for an illustration in a book, a sticker, or a digital image. Interestingly, if you use it in the singular to describe a person, a view, or an object—*"Het is een plaatje!"* (It’s a picture!)—it is a very common Dutch idiom meaning that someone or something is stunningly beautiful or picture-perfect.

kijk.form_note: imperative (command form) of kijken, identical to the verb stem (1st person singular present). In the A2 speaking exam, this instruction tells you to use the pictures on your prompt card to help form your answer.

naar.form_note: fixed preposition used with kijken: 'kijken naar' means 'to look at'. If you reuse 'kijk' in your answer, keep 'naar' with it (e.g., 'Ik kijk naar...').

de.form_note: plural definite article; all plural nouns in Dutch take 'de', even when the singular is a 'het'-word like 'het plaatje'

plaatjes.fast_speech: the /tj/ cluster is usually pronounced like English 'ch': /ˈplaːtʃəs/

sentences.nl: Vertel wat Ricardo doet.
sentences.en: Tell what Ricardo is doing.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **Vertel** (Tell) **wat** (what) **Ricardo** (Ricardo) **doet** (does / is doing).

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Imperative Mood:** *Vertel* is the stem of the verb *vertellen* (to tell). In Dutch, the basic command form (imperative) is simply the verb stem, placed at the very beginning of the sentence without a subject.  
• **Subordinate Clause Word Order:** *Wat Ricardo doet* is an indirect question acting as a subordinate clause. Because it starts with the relative pronoun *wat*, the conjugated verb (*doet*) is pushed to the very end of the clause.  
• **Extensions:**  
– *Vertel wat je wilt.* (Tell [me] what you want.)  
– *Kijk wat hij maakt.* (Look at what he is making.)  
– *Ik weet niet wat Ricardo doet.* (I don't know what Ricardo is doing.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Vraag waar Anna woont. (Ask where Anna lives.)

vertel.form_note: imperative (command form) of 'vertellen' (verb stem). Common in speaking exams to prompt an answer; it introduces an indirect question here.

wat.form_note: interrogative pronoun introducing an indirect question (subordinate clause) after 'Vertel'; sends the conjugated verb 'doet' to the end of the clause.

ricardo.form_note: subject of the subordinate clause 'wat Ricardo doet'. When you answer, start your main clause with 'Ricardo' (or 'Hij') followed immediately by the verb in second position.

doet.form_note: 3rd person singular present tense of 'doen' (stem + t). Placed at the end because 'wat Ricardo doet' is an indirect question. In your answer, either replace 'doet' with a specific action verb in second position (e.g. 'Ricardo kookt') or reuse it.

sentences.nl: Vertel iets over alle plaatjes.
sentences.en: Tell something about all the pictures.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Vertel (Tell) – iets (something) – over (about) – alle (all) – plaatjes (pictures/images).  
• Natural English: Tell something about all the pictures.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Imperative Mood (Gebiedende wijs):** *Vertel* is the imperative (command) form of the verb *vertellen* (to tell). In Dutch, commands start directly with the verb stem (the *ik*-form) with no subject pronoun.  
• **Verb + Preposition:** The verb *vertellen* typically pairs with the preposition *over* when talking *about* a topic (*vertellen over* = to tell about).  
• **Diminutive Plural:** *Plaatjes* is the plural diminutive of *de plaat* (plate/print/image). Diminutives (ending in *-je*) are extremely common in Dutch, and for "picture" or "illustration," the diminutive *het plaatje* is the standard word to use.  
• **Adjective Inflection:** *Al* (all) takes an *-e* ending (*alle*) because it modifies a plural noun (*plaatjes*).  

**Extensions:**  
• *Vertel iets over jezelf.* (Tell something about yourself.)  
• *Lees een verhaal over alle dieren.* (Read a story about all the animals.)  
• *Kijk naar de mooie plaatjes in het boek.* (Look at the pretty pictures in the book.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Schrijf een kort verhaal over alle foto's. (Write a short story about all the photos.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• This exact phrasing is a classic prompt found in the *Inburgeringsexamen* (Dutch civic integration exam) and *Staatsexamen NT2* (Dutch as a second language exam) during the speaking section, where candidates are shown a series of comic strips or photos and asked to narrate what is happening.

plaatjes.form_note: plural of the diminutive noun 'het plaatje' (from 'de plaat' + diminutive suffix -je): all diminutives are het-words in the singular and take -s in the plural

sentences.nl: Ricardo is kapper.

## 1. Literal Translation  
• Ricardo → Ricardo

(Natural English: "Ricardo is a hairdresser/barber.")

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Omitting the Indefinite Article:** In Dutch, when you state someone's profession, nationality, or religion using the verb *zijn* (to be) or *worden* (to become), you drop the indefinite article *een* (a/an). However, if you add an adjective before the profession (e.g., "a *good* barber"), you must bring *een* back: *Ricardo is een goede kapper.*  
• **Gender of Professions:** *Kapper* is the masculine or generic form. If referring specifically to a female hairdresser, Dutch often uses the feminine suffix *-ster*, making it *kapster*.  
• **Extensions:**  
– Mijn broer is leraar. (My brother is a teacher.)  
– Zij wil dokter worden. (She wants to become a doctor.)  
– Hij gaat morgen naar de kapper. (He is going to the hairdresser/barber tomorrow.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Haar vader is bakker in een klein dorp. (Her father is a baker in a small village.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, the word *kapper* is used universally for both men's barbers and women's hair salons. While trendy urban shops might use the English loanword *barbershop* for men, in daily life, everyone simply says *Ik moet naar de kapper* (I need to go to the hairdresser/barber).

sentences.nl: Hij moet het haar wassen.
sentences.en: He has to wash the hair.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Hij (He) + moet (must / has to) + het (the) + haar (hair) + wassen (wash).

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Modal Verbs and Word Order:** *Moet* is the third-person singular form of the modal verb *moeten* (must/have to). In a main clause, the conjugated modal verb sits in the second position, while the main verb (*wassen*) goes to the very end of the sentence in its infinitive form.  
• **Noun Gender:** *Haar* (hair) is a *het*-word (neuter noun) when referring to a mass of hair. Notice that in Dutch, when referring to one's own body parts, you would usually use a possessive pronoun (*zijn haar* - his hair), whereas using *het haar* implies he is washing someone else's hair (e.g., as a hairdresser or a parent) or speaking about hair in a very general, detached way.  
• **Ambiguity Note:** *Haar* also means "her". However, if the sentence meant "He has to wash it for her", the word order would be *Hij moet het voor haar wassen*.  
• **Extensions:**  
– Ik moet de auto wassen. (I have to wash the car.)  
– Zij moet haar handen wassen. (She has to wash her hands.)  
– Wij moeten het huis schoonmaken. (We have to clean the house.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• De kapper moet het haar eerst wassen en daarna knippen. (The hairdresser has to wash the hair first and cut it afterwards.)

wassen.form_note: Infinitive form of 'wassen'. Because of the modal verb 'moet' in second position, this full infinitive is placed at the very end of the sentence.
wassen.fast_speech: The final -n is usually dropped in standard spoken Dutch: /ˈʋɑsə/.

sentences.nl: Hij moet ook het haar knippen.
sentences.en: He also has to cut the hair.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **Hij** (He) **moet** (must / has to) **ook** (also) **het** (the) **haar** (hair) **knippen** (to cut).  
• *Natural English: He also has to cut the hair.*

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Modal Verb Sentence Bracket:** In Dutch, when using a modal verb like *moet* (from *moeten* - must/have to), the conjugated modal verb goes in the second position, and the main verb goes to the very end of the sentence in its infinitive form (*knippen*).  
• **Placement of "ook":** The adverb *ook* (also/too) usually comes right after the conjugated verb in a standard main clause.  
• **De-words vs. Het-words:** *Haar* is a neuter noun, so it takes the article *het* (singular) instead of *de*. Note that while English uses "cut" for everything, Dutch specifies *knippen* for cutting with scissors (as opposed to *snijden*, which is cutting with a knife).

**Extensions:**  
• Ik moet ook de afwas doen. (I also have to do the dishes.)  
• Zij wil het papier knippen. (She wants to cut the paper.)  
• Wij moeten vandaag werken. (We have to work today.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Zij moet morgen ook het gras maaien. (She also has to mow the grass tomorrow.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch, just like in English, it is much more natural to use a possessive pronoun (like *zijn* - his, or *mijn* - my) when talking about body parts, rather than *het* (the). Saying *"het haar"* sounds a bit clinical, as if he is a hairdresser practicing on a mannequin, or cutting hair that isn't attached to anyone. If he is getting his own hair cut, the Dutch use a different structure: *"Hij moet zijn haar laten knippen"* (He has to have his hair cut).

sentences.nl: En hij moet de vloer vegen.
sentences.en: And he has to sweep the floor.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **En** = And  
• **hij** = he  
• **moet** = must / has to  
• **de vloer** = the floor  
• **vegen** = to sweep  

*Chunk-by-chunk:* And – he – must – the floor – sweep.  
*(Natural English: And he has to sweep the floor.)*

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Modal Verbs & Word Order:** *Moet* is the singular form of the modal verb *moeten* (must/have to). In a Dutch main clause, the conjugated modal verb stays in the second position (after the subject *hij*), while the action verb goes to the very end of the sentence in its infinitive form (*vegen*).  
• **Coordinating Conjunction (En):** *En* (and) does not change the standard word order of the sentence that follows it. You can treat it as being in "Position 0," leaving *hij* in Position 1 and *moet* in Position 2.  
• **De-word:** *Vloer* is a common gender noun, so it takes the article *de*.  

**Extensions:**  
• Ik moet de afwas doen. (I have to do the dishes.)  
• En zij moet de hond uitlaten. (And she has to walk the dog.)  
• Wij moeten vandaag de keuken vegen. (We have to sweep the kitchen today.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• En ik moet na het eten de tafel schoonmaken. (And I have to clean the table after dinner.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• This sentence uses a very common Dutch idiom as well: *"Iets onder de vloer/het tapijt vegen"* (to sweep something under the floor/rug), meaning to hide a problem. Also, in Dutch student houses (*studentenhuizen*), chores like *"de vloer vegen"* are strictly tracked on a *"schoonmaakrooster"* (cleaning schedule), and failing to do your part can sometimes result in a small fine towards the house beer fund!

sentences.nl: Ayla gaat haar handen schoonmaken.
sentences.en: Ayla is going to clean her hands.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Ayla = Ayla  
• gaat = goes (is going to)  
• haar = her  
• handen = hands  
• schoonmaken = clean-make (to clean)  

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Future Tense with *gaan*:** Just like "going to" in English, the verb *gaan* is used as an auxiliary verb in the second position to express a near-future action or intention.  
• **Word Order (Verb at the end):** Because *gaat* is the conjugated verb in the second position, the main action verb (*schoonmaken*) must go all the way to the end of the sentence in its full infinitive form.  
• **Separable Verb:** *Schoonmaken* (schoon + maken) is a separable verb. Because it is at the end of the sentence as an infinitive, it stays joined together as one word. (If conjugated in the present tense, it splits: *Ayla maakt haar handen schoon*).  
• **Extensions:**  
– Ik ga het huis schoonmaken. (I am going to clean the house.)  
– Hij gaat zijn auto wassen. (He is going to wash his car.)  
– Wij gaan onze kamer opruimen. (We are going to tidy up our room.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Tom gaat na het koken de keuken schoonmaken. (Tom is going to clean the kitchen after cooking.)  

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• **Nuance Note:** While *handen schoonmaken* is grammatically correct and used when hands are visibly dirty (e.g., covered in mud, paint, or grease) or when using wet wipes, a native Dutch speaker will almost always say *handen wassen* (to wash hands) for normal, everyday hygiene with soap and water.

gaat.form_note: 3rd person singular present tense of 'gaan', placed in the verb-second position; used here as an auxiliary verb with the infinitive 'schoonmaken' at the end to express a future action

haar.form_note: 3rd person singular feminine possessive pronoun, modifying 'handen' and referring back to the subject Ayla
haar.fast_speech: often reduced to /dər/ ('d'r') in casual spoken Dutch

schoonmaken.form_note: infinitive of the separable verb 'schoonmaken' (prefix 'schoon-' + base verb 'maken'); placed at the end of the clause as one word because it is governed by the auxiliary verb 'gaat'
schoonmaken.fast_speech: final -n is usually dropped, and -nm- often assimilates to -m-: /ˈsxoːmaːkə/

grammarHits.explanation: After gaan the separable verb stays whole and goes to the end.

sentences.nl: Kijk naar de plaatjes.

sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Kijk (Look)  
• naar (to / at)  
• de (the)  
• plaatjes (little pictures / illustrations).  
*Natural translation: Look at the pictures.*

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Imperative Mood:** "Kijk" is the imperative (command) form of the verb *kijken* (to look). In Dutch, you form the standard imperative simply by using the verb stem (the *ik*-form) at the beginning of the sentence without a subject.  
• **Verb + Preposition:** In English, you look *at* something, while in Dutch, the fixed combination is *kijken naar* (literally: to look toward/to).  
• **Diminutive Plural:** "Plaatjes" comes from *de plaat* (plate/print/large picture). Adding *-je* makes it diminutive (*het plaatje*), and adding *-s* makes it plural (*de plaatjes*). In everyday Dutch, "plaatje" is the standard word used for an illustration in a book or a digital image.

**Extensions:**  
• Luister naar de leraar. (Listen to the teacher.)  
• Kijk naar mij. (Look at me.)  
• Zoek het juiste plaatje. (Find the correct picture.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Kijk naar de mooie vogels in de tuin. (Look at the beautiful birds in the garden.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• While *het plaatje* literally means a small picture, the singular form is also used idiomatically in Dutch to describe something or someone that looks stunning or picture-perfect. For example, if someone looks great in an outfit, or a house is beautifully decorated, a Dutch person might say: *"Het is echt een plaatje!"* (It really is a picture / It looks gorgeous!).

sentences.nl: Vertel wat Ayla doet.
sentences.en: Tell what Ayla is doing.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Vertel: Tell  
• wat: what  
• Ayla: Ayla  
• doet: does / is doing  

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Imperative Mood:** *Vertel* is the imperative (command) form of the verb *vertellen* (to tell). In Dutch, the singular imperative is simply the verb stem, formed by removing *-en* from the infinitive and adjusting the spelling to keep the short vowel sound (vertellen -> vertel).  
• **Subordinate Clause Word Order:** *Wat Ayla doet* is an indirect question acting as a subordinate clause. In Dutch subordinate clauses, the conjugated verb (*doet*) is pushed to the very end of the clause, rather than staying right after the subject.  
• **Extensions:**  
– Vertel wat je ziet. (Tell [me] what you see.)  
– Kijk wat hij maakt. (Look at what he is making.)  
– Ik weet wat zij bedoelt. (I know what she means.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Vertel waar jullie morgen naartoe gaan. (Tell me where you guys are going tomorrow.)  

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch educational materials, children's books, and language exams (like the *Inburgeringsexamen*), commands like *Vertel wat...* (Tell what...) or *Beschrijf wat...* (Describe what...) are standard prompts. They sound very direct in English without a "please," but in Dutch instructional contexts, this directness is completely neutral and expected.

vertel.form_note: imperative (command form) of 'vertellen', same as the 'ik'-form in the present tense. In the exam, 'Vertel...' introduces an indirect question.
vertel.fast_speech: The 'v' sounds soft (almost like English 'f' or 'v'), and 'er' is a weak schwa sound /vər/.

wat.form_note: interrogative pronoun introducing an indirect question after 'Vertel'. It pushes the conjugated verb ('doet') to the end of the clause.

ayla.form_note: singular proper noun, functions as the subject of the clause. Start your exam answer with 'Ayla' or 'Zij' (She).

doet.form_note: 3rd person singular ('zij') present tense of the irregular verb 'doen' (stem 'doe' + t). Placed at the end because 'wat Ayla doet' is an indirect question. In your answer, replace this with the specific action verb in the second position (e.g., 'Ayla leest een boek').

grammarHits.explanation: Wat doet Ayla? becomes Vertel wat Ayla doet.

sentences.nl: Vertel iets over alle plaatjes.
sentences.en: Tell something about all the pictures.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Vertel (Tell) – iets (something) – over (about) – alle (all) – plaatjes (pictures).  
• Natural translation: Tell something about all the pictures.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Imperative mood (*Gebiedende wijs*):** The sentence starts with *Vertel*, which is the stem of the verb *vertellen* (to tell). This is the standard way to give a command, instruction, or prompt in Dutch.  
• **Verb + Preposition:** The verb *vertellen* is typically paired with the preposition *over* when you mean "to tell about" or "to talk about" a topic.  
• **Diminutive Plural:** *Plaatjes* is the plural diminutive of *de plaat* (plate/print/picture). While *plaat* can mean a vinyl record or a metal sheet, the diminutive *het plaatje* specifically means a small picture, illustration, or image.  
• **Quantifier *Alle*:** *Alle* is the inflected form of *al* (all) and is always used directly before plural nouns (like *plaatjes*) without needing an article like *de*.  
• **Extensions:**  
– *Vertel eens iets over jezelf.* (Tell me something about yourself.)  
– *Ik heb alle boeken gelezen.* (I have read all the books.)  
– *Dit boek heeft mooie plaatjes.* (This book has nice pictures.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Schrijf een kort verhaal over alle foto's. (Write a short story about all the photos.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• This exact phrasing is a staple of the Dutch *Inburgeringsexamen* (civic integration exam) and NT2 (Dutch as a second language) speaking tests. Candidates are frequently shown a storyboard of three or four images (*plaatjes*) and given this exact prompt to test their ability to form coherent, descriptive sentences.

vertel.form_note: imperative (command form) of 'vertellen': equal to the verb stem (infinitive minus -en, double l becomes single l). In A2 speaking exams, this prompts you to describe something. Do not reuse 'vertel' in your answer; instead, start a new main clause describing the pictures (e.g., 'Op het eerste plaatje zie ik...').
vertel.fast_speech: The prefix 'ver-' is unstressed and reduced to /vər/ or /və/.

iets.form_note: indefinite pronoun acting as the direct object of 'vertel'

over.form_note: preposition that goes with the verb 'vertellen' (vertellen over = to tell about)

alle.form_note: inflected form of 'al' (with -e and doubled l to keep the short /ɑ/ sound) used directly before plural nouns. In the exam, this means you must say at least one sentence about every single picture shown.

plaatjes.form_note: plural of 'plaatje' (which is the diminutive of 'de plaat'): all diminutives end in -je and take -s in the plural
plaatjes.fast_speech: The /tj/ cluster is often pronounced like 'ch' in 'church': /ˈplaːtʃəs/.

sentences.nl: Ayla pakt de zeep.
sentences.en: Ayla takes the soap.
sentences.note: Meester's reference answer, built from the topic bank.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Ayla (Ayla) – pakt (grabs/takes) – de (the) – zeep (soap).  
• Natural translation: Ayla grabs the soap.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Word Order:** This sentence uses the standard Subject-Verb-Object (SVO) word order for a simple declarative statement in Dutch.  
• **Verb Conjugation:** *Pakt* comes from the infinitive *pakken* (to grab, to take). For the third-person singular (he/she/it/Ayla) in the present tense, you take the verb stem (*pak*) and add a *-t* (*pakt*).  
• **Noun Gender:** *Zeep* is a common-gender noun, so it takes the definite article *de* (as opposed to neuter nouns, which take *het*). Notice how *zeep* is treated as a singular noun, even though soap is often an uncountable substance in English.  
• **Extensions:**  
  – Hij pakt de sleutels. (He grabs the keys.)  
  – Zij koopt de zeep. (She buys the soap.)  
  – Ik pak een handdoek. (I grab a towel.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Thomas pakt de shampoo en stapt onder de douche. (Thomas grabs the shampoo and steps into the shower.)

ayla.form_note: subject of the sentence, placed in the first position of a standard main clause

pakt.form_note: 3rd person singular present tense of 'pakken' (stem 'pak' + -t); placed in the second position (verb-second word order)
pakt.fast_speech: before 'de', the /t/ is often unreleased or blends into the /d/: /pɑkdə/

de.form_note: definite article for singular common-gender (de-word) nouns like 'zeep'
de.fast_speech: always pronounced with an unstressed schwa /də/

zeep.form_note: singular common-gender noun (de-word), acting as the direct object of 'pakt' (normally uncountable as a substance; plural 'zepen' means 'types/bars of soap': double ee becomes single e in an open syllable, add -en)

sentences.nl: Ze wast haar handen onder de kraan.
sentences.en: She washes her hands under the tap.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **Ze** (She) **wast** (washes) **haar** (her) **handen** (hands) **onder** (under) **de** (the) **kraan** (tap/faucet).  
• Natural translation: She washes her hands under the tap.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Verb Conjugation:** *Wast* comes from the infinitive *wassen* (to wash). The stem is *was*. Normally, the third-person singular (he/she/it) adds a *-t* to the stem, making *wast*.  
• **Possessives with Body Parts:** While Dutch sometimes uses definite articles (*de/het*) with body parts, using the possessive pronoun (*haar handen*) is the standard and most natural way to say "wash one's hands."  
• **Preposition:** *Onder* (under) is used literally here to show the position of the hands relative to the *kraan* (tap).  

**Extensions:**  
• *Hij wast zijn gezicht met koud water.* (He washes his face with cold water.)  
• *Zet de emmer maar onder de kraan.* (Just put the bucket under the tap.)  
• *Vergeet niet je handen te wassen.* (Don't forget to wash your hands.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• *De kok wast de verse groenten onder de koude kraan.* (The chef washes the fresh vegetables under the cold tap.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In traditional Dutch homes, the small toilet room (*het kleinste kamertje*) Usually only has a tiny sink (*fonteintje*) with a tap that only runs cold water, meant strictly for a quick hand rinse.  
• Dutch tap water (*kraanwater*) is among the cleanest in the world; locals drink it straight from the tap and rarely buy bottled water at home.

ze.form_note: unstressed subject pronoun, 3rd person singular feminine (stressed form: zij); takes first position in the sentence

wast.form_note: 3rd person singular present tense of wassen (stem was + t); in verb-second position right after the subject

haar.form_note: possessive pronoun, 3rd person singular feminine, modifying 'handen'
haar.fast_speech: often reduced to /dər/ (spelled d'r) in everyday speech

handen.form_note: plural of hand: add -en; direct object of 'wast'

onder.form_note: preposition of place introducing the phrase 'onder de kraan'

de.form_note: definite article for singular common-gender (de-word) nouns like 'kraan'

kraan.form_note: singular common-gender noun (de-word), object of the preposition 'onder'

sentences.nl: En ze droogt haar handen af met een handdoek.
sentences.en: And she dries her hands with a towel.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• En (And)  
• ze (she)  
• droogt (dries)  
• haar handen (her hands)  
• af (off - *separable verb prefix*)  
• met (with)  
• een handdoek (a towel).

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Separable Verb (*afdrogen*):** The verb used here is *afdrogen* (to dry off). In a main clause in the present tense, the prefix (*af*) detaches from the verb stem (*droogt*) and moves to the end of the core clause, right after the direct object (*haar handen*).  
• **Preposition Placement:** Prepositional phrases like *met een handdoek* (with a towel) can be placed after the separated prefix (*af*). Calling this "putting it in the *naveld* (post-field)" is common in Dutch grammar; it makes the sentence easier to process.  
• **Possessive Pronouns with Body Parts:** Unlike some European languages that use definite articles (e.g., "the hands"), Dutch uses possessive pronouns (*haar handen*) when referring to one's own body parts, just like English.

**Extensions:**  
• Hij wast zijn gezicht met koud water. (He washes his face with cold water.)  
• Ik droog de borden meteen af. (I dry the plates off immediately.)  
• Droog jij de tafel even af met een doekje? (Will you dry off the table for a second with a cloth?)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Hij maakt zijn schoenen schoon met een borstel. (He cleans his shoes with a brush.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• **Compound Words & The "Theedoek":** In Dutch, *handdoek* literally means "hand cloth," though it is used as the general word for bath towels as well. In a Dutch kitchen, however, you will always find two distinct towels hanging side by side: a *handdoek* (specifically for drying your hands) and a *theedoek* (tea towel, strictly for drying dishes). Using the *theedoek* to dry your hands is a minor household faux pas in the Netherlands!

en.form_note: coordinating conjunction connecting this sentence to the previous one; it takes position 0, so the normal subject-verb order (ze droogt) follows
en.fast_speech: often reduced to /ən/ or /n/

droogt.form_note: 3rd person singular present tense of the separable verb 'afdrogen' (stem 'droog' + -t); placed in second position (verb-second rule), while the prefix 'af' moves to the end of the main clause

haar.form_note: 3rd person singular feminine possessive determiner, modifying 'handen'
haar.fast_speech: often reduced to /dər/ ('d'r') in casual speech

handen.form_note: plural of hand: add -en; acts as the direct object of 'afdrogen'

af.form_note: separable prefix of the verb 'afdrogen', placed after the direct object at the end of the core clause

met.form_note: preposition indicating the instrument used ('with a towel')

een.form_note: indefinite article used before singular countable nouns (both de- and het-words)
een.fast_speech: pronounced with a schwa /ən/, not like the number 'één' (/eːn/)

handdoek.form_note: singular compound noun (hand + doek), de-word; object of the preposition 'met'
handdoek.fast_speech: spelled with double 'dd', but pronounced as a single /d/: /ˈɦɑnduk/

sentences.nl: Lucie heeft deze spullen gekocht.
sentences.en: Lucie bought these things.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Lucie (Lucie) heeft (has) deze (these) spullen (things/stuff) gekocht (bought).  
• Natural translation: Lucie bought this stuff. / Lucie has bought these things.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Present Perfect Tense (Voltooide Tijd):** Dutch uses the present perfect much more frequently than English to describe completed past actions. It requires an auxiliary verb—here *heeft* (from *hebben*, to have)—in the second position, and the past participle *gekocht* (from *kopen*, to buy) at the very end of the sentence.  
• **Word Order (De Tangconstructie):** Notice how the verbs *heeft* and *gekocht* act like pincers, wrapping around the direct object (*deze spullen*).  
• **Demonstrative Pronoun (*Deze*):** *Spullen* (stuff/things/belongings) is always plural in this context. Plural nouns always take the common gender article *de*, which means the word for "these" must be *deze* (as opposed to *dit*, which is only for singular *het*-words).  

• **Extensions:**  
– Ik heb nieuwe schoenen gekocht. (I bought new shoes.)  
– Waar heb je deze spullen gevonden? (Where did you find this stuff?)  
– Hij heeft dat boek gisteren gelezen. (He read that book yesterday.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Mijn broer heeft al zijn oude spullen verkocht. (My brother sold all of his old stuff.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• The word *spullen* is an essential, everyday Dutch word. While it translates to "things" or "stuff," it specifically refers to personal belongings or physical items. You will often see it in the compound word *spullenbak* (a bin for random items) or hear people talk about selling their old *spullen* on Vrijmarkt (the nationwide street market on King's Day) or via Marktplaats (the Dutch equivalent of eBay/Craigslist).

lucie.form_note: subject of the sentence, placed in the first position

heeft.meaning: has (used with 'gekocht' to form the present perfect tense: 'bought' / 'has bought')
heeft.form_note: 3rd person singular present tense of 'hebben'; placed in the second position (verb-second rule) as the auxiliary verb for the present perfect
heeft.fast_speech: the final -t can be dropped before a consonant: /ɦeːf/

deze.form_note: used before 'de'-words in the singular and all plural nouns (here modifying the plural noun 'spullen')

spullen.form_note: plural of 'spul': double the final consonant 'l' to keep the vowel 'u' short, then add -en (in modern Dutch, almost exclusively used in the plural)

gekocht.form_note: irregular past participle of 'kopen'; placed at the very end of the main clause

sentences.nl: Vertel welke spullen dat zijn.
sentences.en: Tell which things those are.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Vertel (Tell) welke (which) spullen (stuff / things) dat (that/those) zijn (are).  
• Natural English: "Tell me which things those are."

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Imperative:** *Vertel* is the command form (imperative) of the verb *vertellen* (to tell). It is formed simply by using the verb stem.  
• **Subordinate Clause Word Order:** *Welke spullen dat zijn* is an indirect question acting as a subordinate clause. Because of this, the conjugated verb (*zijn*) is kicked to the very end of the sentence.  
• **Singular Pronoun with Plural Verb:** In Dutch, the singular demonstrative pronoun *dat* (that) or *dit* (this) is used to introduce or point out plural nouns when linked by the verb *zijn* (are). Even though *spullen* is plural and *zijn* is plural, *dat* remains singular.  
• **Plural-only Noun:** *Spullen* (stuff/things/belongings) is almost always used in the plural form in this context. (The singular *spul* translates more closely to "substance" or "material").  
• **Extensions:**  
  – *Laat zien welke boeken dat zijn.* (Show [me] which books those are.)  
  – *Ik weet niet wiens spullen dat zijn.* (I don't know whose stuff that is.)  
  – *Vertel wat je gisteren hebt gedaan.* (Tell [me] what you did yesterday.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Vertel me welke schoenen je wilt kopen. (Tell me which shoes you want to buy.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Using the bare imperative (*Vertel...*) is grammatically correct, can sound quite direct or bossy in spoken Dutch, like an interrogation. In everyday conversation, Dutch speakers almost always soften commands using modal particles like *eens* or *even*, or by adding the indirect object *me* (me). A much more natural, friendly way a native would say this is: *"Vertel eens welke spullen dat zijn."*

vertel.form_note: imperative (command form) singular of 'vertellen', equal to the ik-form in the present tense; frequently used in A2 speaking-exam prompts to introduce an indirect question
vertel.fast_speech: initial /v/ is often pronounced closer to /f/: /fərˈtɛl/

welke.form_note: inflected with -e because it modifies the plural noun 'spullen' (used for all plural nouns and singular de-words); introduces the indirect question (subordinate clause) after 'Vertel'

spullen.form_note: plural of het spul: double the consonant 'l' to keep the short /ʏ/ vowel, then add -en; almost always used in the plural to mean 'things/stuff'

dat.form_note: singular neuter form 'dat' used as an introductory/pointing subject ('those') with the linking verb 'zijn', even though it refers to the plural noun 'spullen' (a standard Dutch pattern: 'Dat zijn mijn spullen' = 'Those are my things')

zijn.form_note: irregular verb 'zijn', 3rd person plural present tense (agrees in number with the plural noun 'spullen'); placed at the very end of the sentence because 'welke ...' after 'Vertel' is an indirect question (subordinate clause). When you answer in the exam, reuse this verb in second position: 'Dat zijn ...'

grammarHits.explanation: zijn moves to the end after welke spullen.

sentences.nl: Vertel ook wat Lucie erin kan doen.
sentences.en: Also tell what Lucie can put in them.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Vertel (Tell) / ook (also) / wat (what) / Lucie (Lucie) / erin (there-in / in it) / kan (can) / doen (do).  
• Natural translation: Also tell what Lucie can put/do in it.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Imperative (Command):** *Vertel* is the stem of *vertellen* (to tell), placed at the very beginning of the sentence to give a direct instruction.  
• **Subordinate Clause Word Order:** The word *wat* introduces an indirect question (subordinate clause), which pushes all the verbs (*kan doen*) to the very end of the sentence.  
• **Pronominal Adverb (*erin*):** In Dutch, you don't say *in het* (in it) for objects. Instead, *het* becomes *er* and merges with the preposition: *er + in = erin* (in it).  
• **Idiom (*erin doen*):** While *doen* literally means "to do," when combined with a location or container (*erin*), it commonly translates to "to put in" (e.g., putting ingredients into a bowl or items into a bag).  

**Extensions:**  
• *Laat zien wat je ermee kunt maken.* (Show what you can make with it.)  
• *Ik weet niet wat ik erin moet doen.* (I don't know what I have to put in it.)  
• *Vraag ook wie er morgen kan komen.* (Also ask who can come tomorrow.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Leg ook uit wat we ermee kunnen doen. (Also explain what we can do with it.)

vertel.form_note: imperative (command form) of 'vertellen', same form as the 1st person singular ('ik vertel'). In the A2 speaking exam, 'Vertel...' introduces an indirect question, pushing the verbs in the next clause to the end. To answer, turn that indirect clause back into a normal main clause.
vertel.fast_speech: The prefix 'ver-' is unstressed and reduced to /vər/ or /fər/.

ook.form_note: adverb adding a second task to the exam prompt; invariant form.

wat.form_note: interrogative pronoun introducing an indirect question (subordinate clause) after 'Vertel'. Because 'wat' starts a subordinate clause, the verbs ('kan doen') must go to the very end of the sentence.

lucie.form_note: proper noun, subject of the subordinate clause. In your answer, start with 'Lucie' (or 'Zij'/'Ze') followed immediately by the verb 'kan' (verb-second rule).

erin.form_note: pronominal adverb combining 'er' (it/them) + 'in' (in); replaces 'in + thing/things'. Forms a fixed expression with 'doen': 'ergens iets in doen' (to put something into something). Reuse 'erin' in your answer right before 'doen' (e.g., 'Zij kan ... erin doen').
erin.fast_speech: The 'e' is often reduced to a schwa: /ərˈɪn/.

kan.form_note: 3rd person singular present tense of the irregular modal verb 'kunnen' (matches the subject 'Lucie'). It is at the end of the sentence because of the indirect question 'wat...'. In your answer (a main clause), move 'kan' to the second position: 'Lucie kan...'.

doen.form_note: infinitive of 'doen'. Combined with 'erin' ('ergens iets in doen'), it means 'to put into'. Because it is paired with the modal verb 'kan', 'doen' stays as an infinitive at the very end of the sentence—both in this indirect question and in your main-clause answer.

grammarHits.explanation: kan doen at the end; erin = in it / in them.

sentences.nl: Gebruik alle plaatjes.
sentences.en: Use all the pictures.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Gebruik (Use)  
• alle (all)  
• plaatjes (little-pictures / images).

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Imperative Mood:** *Gebruik* is the imperative (command) form of the verb *gebruiken* (to use). For standard commands in Dutch, you simply use the verb stem (the *ik*-form) at the very beginning of the sentence without a subject pronoun.  
• **Inflected "al":** The word *al* (all) takes an *-e* ending (*alle*) when it comes directly before a plural noun (*plaatjes*) or a singular common-gender (*de*) noun.  
• **Diminutive Plural:** *Plaatjes* is the plural diminutive of *plaat* (plate/print/picture). While the *-je* suffix literally makes things small, *plaatje* is simply the standard everyday Dutch word for an illustration, image, or picture in a book or on a screen.  
• **Extensions:**  
– Bekijk alle foto's. (Look at all the photos.)  
– Gebruik je eigen woorden. (Use your own words.)  
– Lees alle zinnen hardop. (Read all the sentences out loud.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Kies alle juiste antwoorden om door te gaan. (Choose all the correct answers to continue.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• **Sparen voor plaatjes:** In the Netherlands, the word *plaatjes* is culturally synonymous with supermarket promotional campaigns—most famously the historical nature albums by Albert Heijn (originally launched in the 1920s with educator Jac. P. Thijsse, and still revived today). Shoppers receive packs of stickers/cards (*plaatjes*) with their groceries to glue into an educational album, making "Mag ik de plaatjes?" (Can I have the picture cards?) a classic phrase heard from Dutch children outside supermarkets.

gebruik.form_note: imperative (command form) of 'gebruiken': uses the verb stem (same as the 'ik' form in present tense). Often seen in exam instructions; you don't repeat this verb in your answer, you just follow the instruction.

alle.form_note: inflected form of 'al' with an -e ending because it comes directly before a plural noun ('plaatjes'); in Dutch, you do not put 'de' after 'alle'
word_forms: base form: al (e.g., al het water)

plaatjes.form_note: plural of 'plaatje' (which is the diminutive of 'de plaat'): all diminutives end in -je and take -s in the plural

sentences.nl: Dat zijn een laptoptas, een toilettasje en een koffer.
sentences.en: Those are a laptop bag, a small toiletry bag, and a suitcase.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Dat (That / Those) + zijn (are) + een (a) + laptoptas (laptop bag), + een (a) + toilettasje (little toiletry bag) + en (and) + een (a) + koffer (suitcase).  
• Natural translation: Those are a laptop bag, a toiletry bag, and a suitcase.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **"Dat zijn" for "Those are":** In Dutch, when pointing out or introducing plural things, the singular pronouns *dit* (this) and *dat* (that) are combined with the plural verb *zijn* (are). You do not use the plural demonstratives (*deze/die*) in this specific introductory structure.  
• **Compound Nouns:** Dutch writes compound nouns together as one word, such as *laptoptas* (laptop + bag) and *toilettas* (toilet + bag).  
• **Diminutives (*-je*):** *Toilettasje* ends in *-je*, making it diminutive (a small bag). All diminutives in Dutch are *het*-words, though the indefinite article remains *een* (a/an).  
• **Extensions:**  
  – Dat zijn mijn nieuwe koffers. (Those are my new suitcases.)  
  – Dit zijn een paspoort en een vliegticket. (These are a passport and a plane ticket.)  
  – Ik zoek een klein tasje voor de reis. (I am looking for a small bag for the trip.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Dat zijn een rugzak, een paspoortje en een reiskoffer. (Those are a backpack, a little passport, and a travel suitcase.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• **Love for Diminutives:** Dutch speakers use diminutives (words ending in *-je*, *-tje*, *-pje*) constantly, not just to indicate physical size, but also because it sounds friendlier or simply because it is the standard term for an object. For example, a toiletry bag is almost always referred to as a *toilettasje* rather than a *toilettas*, regardless of how big it actually is.

dat.form_note: Demonstrative pronoun used as a dummy subject to introduce or point to things. In Dutch, 'dat' remains singular in form even when followed by a plural verb ('zijn') and plural or multiple items.

sentences.nl: Haar computer, toiletspullen en kleren.
sentences.en: Her computer, toiletries, and clothes.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Haar (Her) computer, (computer,) toiletspullen (toiletries / toilet-things) en (and) kleren (clothes).

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Listing Rule (No Oxford Comma):** Like in English, items in a Dutch list are separated by commas. However, in Dutch, you generally **do not** use a comma before the word *en* (and) at the end of a simple list.  
• **Compound Nouns:** *Toiletspullen* is a compound noun made of *toilet* + *spullen* (things/stuff). In Dutch, compound nouns are written together as a single word.  
• **Plurals and Synonyms:** *Kleren* is the everyday plural word for "clothes." You might also see *kleding*, which is an uncountable singular noun meaning "clothing."  
• **Extensions:**  
  – Mijn paspoort, telefoon en sleutels. (My passport, phone, and keys.)  
  – Vergeet je kampeerspullen niet. (Don't forget your camping gear/stuff.)  
  – Hij wast zijn eigen kleren. (He washes his own clothes.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Zij pakt haar laptop, schrijfmateriaal en boeken in voor school. (She packs her laptop, stationery, and books for school.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• The word *spullen* (things/stuff/gear) is extremely common and versatile in everyday Dutch. Instead of using formal words for specific categories of items, the Dutch love to simply attach *spullen* to the end of a word. For example: *schoolspullen* (school supplies), * gymschoenen en sportspullen* (gym shoes and sports gear), or *keukenspullen* (kitchenware).

sentences.nl: Twee tassen en een koffer.
sentences.en: Two bags and a suitcase.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Twee (Two)  
• tassen (bags)  
• en (and)  
• een (a / one)  
• koffer (suitcase)  

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Noun Plurals & Spelling:** The singular form of "tassen" is *tas* (bag). When forming the plural with *-en*, the consonant 's' is doubled to keep the vowel 'a' short (*tas* → *tassen*).  
• **Articles and Numbers:** In Dutch, the word *een* means both the indefinite article "a/an" and the number "one". When you want to specifically emphasize the number "one" (as opposed to two), it is written with accents: *één* (e.g., *twee tassen en één koffer*).  
• **Extensions:**  
  – Drie koffers en een rugzak. (Three suitcases and a backpack.)  
  – Ik heb twee tassen bij me. (I have two bags with me.)  
  – Een grote koffer en een kleine tas. (A big suitcase and a small bag.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Wij reizen met één grote koffer en twee kleine tassen. (We are traveling with one big suitcase and two small bags.)

en.form_note: coordinating conjunction connecting the two noun phrases 'twee tassen' and 'een koffer'

sentences.nl: Ze kan daar papieren, make-up en schoenen in doen.
sentences.en: She can put papers, makeup, and shoes in there.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **Ze** – She  
• **kan** – can  
• **daar** – there  
• **papieren,** – papers,  
• **make-up** – makeup  
• **en** – and  
• **schoenen** – shoes  
• **in** – in  
• **doen.** – do / put.  

(Natural English: "She can put papers, makeup, and shoes in there.")

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Pronominal Adverb Splitting (*daarin*):** In Dutch, you don't say "in it/that" (*in dat*). Instead, *dat + in* becomes **daarin** (therein / in there). As seen in this sentence, *daarin* is very often split up, with the objects placed right in the middle: **daar** + [objects] + **in**.  
• **Modal Verb Word Order:** The conjugated modal verb **kan** (can) sits in the second position, which pushes the main infinitive verb **doen** all the way to the end of the sentence.  
• **Idiom (*ergens iets in doen*):** While *doen* literally means "to do", when combined with *in* (or *op/bij*), it functions as a casual, everyday way to say "to put."  

**Extensions:**  
• *Ik wil **daar** mijn boeken **in doen**.* (I want to put my books in there.)  
• *Kun je **daar** wat suiker **bij doen**?* (Can you put/add some sugar in with that?)  
• *Hij **doet** zijn telefoon **in** zijn zak.* (He puts his phone in his pocket.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• *We kunnen daar onze jassen en tassen in doen.* (We can put our coats and bags in there.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• **Positional Verbs vs. *Doen*:** Dutch is famous for forcing speakers to choose specific "positional" verbs for "to put"—such as *zetten* (put upright), *leggen* (put flat), or *stoppen* (stuff/tuck inside). However, when listing random items of different shapes (like flat papers, upright shoes, and small makeup), using **in doen** is a very natural Dutch "hack" to avoid choosing between *leggen* and *zetten*!

sentences.nl: Ik zie een laptoptas, een toilettas en een koffer.
sentences.en: I see a laptop bag, a toiletry bag, and a suitcase.
sentences.note: Meester's reference answer, built from the topic bank.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Ik (I) zie (see) een (a) laptoptas (laptop-bag), een (a) toilettas (toiletry-bag) en (and) een (a) koffer (suitcase).  
• Natural translation: I see a laptop bag, a toiletry bag, and a suitcase.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Compound Nouns:** Dutch frequently glues words together to make a single noun. While English uses two words ("laptop bag" and "toiletry bag"), Dutch combines them into *laptoptas* and *toilettas*. The gender of a compound noun is always determined by the last word (since *tas* is a *de*-word, both compounds are *de*-words).  
• **Indefinite Article (*een*):** Unlike the definite articles (*de* and *het*), the indefinite article *een* ("a" or "an") is the same for all singular nouns, regardless of gender.  
• **Irregular Verb (*zien*):** *Zie* is the first-person singular (ik) present tense form of the irregular verb *zien* (to see).  
• **No Oxford Comma:** In Dutch lists, you generally do not place a comma before the word *en* (and).  

**Extensions:**  
• Ik zoek een handtas en een rugzak. (I am looking for a handbag and a backpack.)  
• Zie jij mijn koffer? (Do you see my suitcase?)  
• Hij koopt een nieuwe sporttas. (He is buying a new gym bag.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Ik pak een rugzak, een toilettas en een grote koffer voor de vakantie. (I am packing a backpack, a toiletry bag, and a large suitcase for the vacation.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch, the word *toilet* is pronounced similarly to the French way (twah-LET), and in *toilettas*, it simply refers to personal grooming/washing items. It does not carry the slightly jarring literal meaning that "toilet bag" has in American English.

sentences.nl: Ze kan haar laptop in de laptoptas doen.
sentences.en: She can put her laptop in the laptop bag.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Ze = She  
• kan = can  
• haar = her  
• laptop = laptop  
• in = in / into  
• de = the  
• laptoptas = laptop bag (laptop + bag)  
• doen = do / put  

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Modal Verbs and Word Order:** When using a modal verb like *kunnen* (can/to be able to), the conjugated modal verb (*kan*) goes in the second position of the sentence, and the main verb (*doen*) is pushed to the very end in its infinitive form.  
• **Idiomatic use of "doen":** While *doen* literally means "to do", in Dutch it is very commonly used with the preposition *in* to mean "to put inside" (especially with bags, boxes, or containers), alongside the verb *stoppen*.  
• **Compound Nouns:** Dutch combines nouns to make new ones. *Laptop* + *tas* becomes *laptoptas* (one word).  
• **Extensions:**  
  – Ik kan mijn sleutels niet in mijn zak doen. (I cannot put my keys in my pocket.)  
  – Kun je de melk in de koelkast doen? (Can you put the milk in the fridge?)  
  – Hij wil zijn boeken in de rugzak doen. (He wants to put his books in the backpack.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Hij kan zijn telefoon in zijn jaszak doen. (He can put his phone in his coat pocket.)  

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Because the Dutch commute almost everywhere by bicycle—often in rainy weather—having a sturdy, waterproof *laptoptas* or backpack is an essential part of daily work and student life in the Netherlands.

sentences.nl: Ze kan haar tandenborstel in de toilettas doen.
sentences.en: She can put her toothbrush in the toiletry bag.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **Ze** (She) **kan** (can) **haar** (her) **tandenborstel** (toothbrush) **in** (in) **de** (the) **toilettas** (toiletry bag) **doen** (do/put).  
• Natural translation: She can put her toothbrush in the toiletry bag.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Modal Verbs and Word Order:** This sentence uses the modal verb *kunnen* (can/to be able to), conjugated as *kan* in the second position. In Dutch, when you use a modal verb, the main action verb goes to the very end of the sentence in its infinitive form (*doen*). This creates a "verb bracket" around the rest of the information.  
• **Idiomatic use of *doen*:** While *doen* literally means "to do," Dutch speakers very frequently use it to mean "to put" when placing something inside a container, bag, or space (combined with the preposition *in*).  
• **Compound Nouns:** Both *tandenborstel* (*tanden* [teeth] + *borstel* [brush]) and *toilettas* (*toilet* [toilet/grooming] + *tas* [bag]) are compound nouns. In Dutch, these are always written together as one word, and the last word determines the gender/article (e.g., *de tas* -> *de toilettas*).  

**Extensions:**  
• Ik **kan** mijn sleutels **in** mijn jaszak **doen**. (I can put my keys in my coat pocket.)  
• Kun je wat suiker **in** mijn koffie **doen**? (Can you put some sugar in my coffee?)  
• Hij **kan** zijn boeken **in** de rugzak **doen**. (He can put his books in the backpack.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• We kunnen de vuile kleren in de wasmachine doen. (We can put the dirty clothes in the washing machine.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch, the word *toilet* in compounds like *toilettas* or *toiletspullen* (toiletries) refers to the older French meaning of personal grooming and washing up, rather than the actual toilet bowl. Taking a well-stocked *toilettas* is a staple of the very popular Dutch camping culture, where people walk across the campsite to the shared *toiletgebouw* (sanitary block) with their bag under their arm.

sentences.nl: En ze kan haar kleren in de koffer doen.
sentences.en: And she can put her clothes in the suitcase.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **En** = And  
• **ze** = she  
• **kan** = can  
• **haar kleren** = her clothes  
• **in de koffer** = in the suitcase  
• **doen.** = do (meaning: *put*).  
*(Full literal: And she can her clothes in the suitcase do.)*

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Modal Verb Word Order (Verb Bracket):** When using a modal verb like *kan* (can), it takes the second position in the main clause, while the main infinitive verb (*doen*) is pushed to the very end of the sentence.Note that starting a sentence with *En* (And) does not change the standard subject-verb word order (*ze kan*).  
• **Idiomatic use of "doen":** While *doen* literally means "to do," Dutch speakers very frequently use it with prepositions (*in*, *op*, *uit*, *aan*) as a casual way to say "to put" or "to place."  
• **Kleren vs. Kleding:** *Kleren* is a plural noun meaning "clothes" (everyday usage). *Kleding* is a singular mass noun meaning "clothing" (slightly more formal).  
• **Extensions:**  
  – Ik **kan** de boodschappen **in** de tas **doen**. (I can put the groceries in the bag.)  
  – Wil jij wat suiker **in** mijn koffie **doen**? (Do you want to put some sugar in my coffee?)  
  – Hij **kan** zijn boeken op tafel **doen**. (He can put his books on the table.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• En hij kan zijn laptop in de rugzak doen. (And he can put his laptop in the backpack.)
